    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Prefer to listen? To hear this entire conversation, and more episodes in the weeks ahead, follow Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts.

    The U.S. Senate just cleared the way for passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, more commonly referred to as BAAJA. The law aims to shorten review timelines for infrastructure projects and protect permits from later revocation, among other provisions. But beyond the technical details, the law has been notable for the unusual coalitions that have arranged in favor and opposed to it: Oil and gas companies, manufacturers, and labor unions are broadly in support, while environmental groups such as the Sierra Club and the Wilderness Society and progressive groups such as the NAACP have lined up against.

    What exactly would BAAJA do? Why has the law divided some trade unions against progressives? And can renewable energy outcompete fossil fuels on the free market?

    The U.S. Senate just cleared the way for passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, more commonly referred to as BAAJA. The law aims to shorten review timelines for infrastructure projects and protect permits from later revocation, among other provisions. But beyond the technical details, the law has been notable for the unusual coalitions that have arranged in favor and opposed to it: Oil and gas companies, manufacturers, and labor unions are broadly in support, while environmental groups such as the Sierra Club and the Wilderness Society and progressive groups such as the NAACP have lined up against.

    Recent findings suggest that what exactly would BAAJA do? Why has the law divided some trade unions against progressives? And can renewable energy outcompete fossil fuels on the free market?

    Those are just a few of the questions that came up in my recent conversation with FP economics columnist Adam Tooze on the podcast we co-host, Ones and Tooze. What follows is an excerpt, edited for length and clarity. For the full conversation, look for Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts. And check out Adam’s Substack newsletter.

    In a recent development, cameron Abadi: What exactly would BAAJA do? And why is this just such a massive concern right now in the United States?

    Adam Tooze: It’s basically an effort to streamline environmental review, restrict certain legal challenges, make permits—once they are issued—more secure. So, enabling investors to proceed robustly. And it’s aiming basically to enable a more rapid build-out of the electricity transmission system.

    It’s such a major deal because this is a really big problem. Electricity interconnection is a fiendishly difficult technical and legal glitch. The Berkeley Lab found that about 2,600 gigawatts of generation and storage projects were seeking grid connection at the end of 2023. And more will have come online since. That’s about twice the existing capacity of the United States’ system. And they spend about five years at least applying for interconnection and entering commercial operation, compared to two years only as recently as a few decades ago. You’ve got projects like a giant wind project in New Mexico, which is supposed to be a transmission line that connects New Mexico to Arizona. It took roughly 17 years from initial development to construction, and the vast majority of that was in the permitting. Pipelines are notorious for exactly the same reasons. So, Mountain Valley Pipeline, which is a gas pipeline 303 miles [long through West Virginia and Virginia], originally billed at $3.5 billion and now finally opened in 2024 at a cost of about $8 billion.

    So there are a fundamental set of concerns about not only how American procedures decide whether they are for or against massive infrastructure projects but also how long it takes them and how expensive they are. If we had a streamlined process, you could process a bunch of obstructions, do it quickly, make a decision, move on. And instead, we have sort of the worst of both worlds, which is a lack of coherence, political chops, and changes by administrations, which are very pro-renewable energy, for instance, and then very opposed to it—which means that even when you do get the permits, they’re not secure. So it’s a mess.

    And this is a mess also against the backdrop of the last effort to break this impasse, which after all was the Biden administration. It’s certainly true now that AI is driving the conversation about the build-out of power supply in the United States. But the conversation started earlier with the push around Bidenomics, which then was instantiated in the form of the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022. And people like Brian Deese, who was a key architect of green industrial policy under the Biden administration, have mentioned that, you know, passing the Inflation Reduction Act without permitting reform produced modest results. Passing the Inflation Reduction Act with permitting reform would have made a huge difference. Passing the permitting reform two years before the Inflation Reduction Act had come into effect, setting the stage for the energy and the money that poured through the Inflation Reduction Act, would have been a complete game-changer. In other words, the pace of rollout would have been very dramatic. And I think that, in a sense, is what this conversation currently is about.

    Industry observers note that and it’s furthermore crucial because it does expose fault lines within the coalitions that you might think of as being supportive to this. So Bidenomics glued a coalition together around the green energy project, around American reindustrialization, but also through extraordinarily complex coalition deals—the “everything bagel” liberalism, patching in a whole variety of different environmental justice groups, activists on behalf of rural America, activists on the behalf of minorities in the United States and underrepresented and discriminated-against communities—and they were all part of the Biden package. [Donald] Trump has blown that up. And what we’re seeing here is also a debate, I think, about what are the terms going to be under which a new, energized Democratic majority actually attempts to restart the project of green modernization in the United States. That’s why this matters beyond the technicalities.

    CA: We tend to think of the left and unions as a natural coalition. But have there always been tensions between them that run along the fault lines of environmentalism, and is that what’s getting revealed in the debate around this law?

    Sources indicate that AT: In support of what I think is called BAAJA, you do see an unusually broad coalition of organized labor. It isn’t just building trade unions—sort of, you know, construction-happy pipeline workers or whatever. It is in fact a very broad coalition, including the AFL-CIO. And so, from their point of view, this is clearly an industrial, productivist kind of strategy. And it makes sense, and they’re not wrong. And the estimates are that this would move significant volumes of investment. Not stupendous, not dramatic. If you’ve actually seen the econometrics on this, the numbers are not overwhelming. But they’re real, and every little bit helps. And the obstruction around these complications has been highly significant in a number of individual cases. So the coalition is real.

    But you’re right, there are also blocking oppositionists. In fact, it’s telling that in the Senate vote on the legislation so far the purple state senators—so senators who are exposed to more competitive races—were notably more supportive of this legislation than those in absolutely solid blue Democratic constituencies, where the leverage of other interests really came to the fore. And there are at least two that are very well worth taking seriously that have been articulated.

    Industry observers note that one is Bill McKibben, one of the real warhorses of the climate movement in the United States, who mentioned, look, it’s all very well to say that we need an energy transition, so we need more electrical generation capacity and transmission facilities. This is clear. It is true. On the other hand, ultimately what counts here is the level of emissions. And so, more construction, more activity in this realm, is not an unalloyed and unambiguous benefit. And if it’s possible that these changes might in fact open the door to large-scale fossil build-out, then, in fact, this is really an ambiguous a set of proposals. And it’s quite clear that in its bipartisan nature, a little bit like some of the Biden administration legislation as well, they are trying to provide pork and trying to buy support from energy interests across the board.

    And then the other constituency that you might think of as left is represented by a spokesperson like Abigail Dillen of Earthjustice, who is representing what in the American conversation is called an environmental justice point of view, first and foremost. And so, just for clarification’s sake, environmental politics is a very broad church. Climate politics within that comes in different shades as well, but climate politics has this very macroscopic, ultimately global point of view. And one of the answers given by the establishment with regards to climate politics is simply electrify everything, build as much clean energy infrastructure as possible as rapidly as possible. But the consequences of that locally can of course be very, very disruptive, not to say incredibly damaging. And this is where the environmental justice movement comes in in the United States, which has a genealogy which really originates in the 1980s and 1990s, centrally concerned with the interests of marginalized communities in the United States, notably Black communities in the American South, who find themselves systematically in harm’s way when it comes to otherwise perhaps interesting and vital industrial expansion. And so her argument, and the opposition of environmental justice campaigners around this, is to say, well, it’s all very well that you open the door to this kind of development, but who walks through that door? Which interests are going to take advantage of this, and who is going to lose out?

    According to recent reports, and to go back to your big-picture historical question, what you’re seeing there is a confrontation between, if you like, three generations of American radical and progressive politics. One is the classic New Deal productivist coalition, which is about a bigger government and facilitating public-private partnerships in various ways that enable large-scale investment and development. And that had very considerable buy-in from trade unions.

    Industry observers note that expanding the U.S. grid is vital to staying globally competitive.

    But what we see from the 1960s onward—not necessarily in hostility to organized labor but recognizing the impact of the success of this kind of development and its lopsidedness and its egalitarian tendencies—are the other two constituencies of American progressivism, which are now speaking their voice. These things didn’t emerge at the same time in the 1930s, but you could say in the 1960s we see the development of the ecological movement in the United States, the broad-based opposition to environmental damage, which in many cases has a distinctly upper-middle-class, Sierra Club kind of feel to it.

    According to recent reports, and then from the late 1970s, 1980s, onward, the environmental justice movement, which is in a sense environmental politics crossed with the Civil Rights Movement in the United States and focusing on environmental issues. And those three things together come out of the same tradition of American progressivism, you might say, but they are not necessarily on the same page. And their targets are not necessarily the same thing either. And the work that Bidenomics did was to, in some senses, square that circle. And as we’ve said, that’s the coalition that needs to be rebuilt. And this is a conversation about how that gets done.

    It has been revealed that CA: One often hears that renewables now outcompete other sources of energy on economic terms. So why shouldn’t advocates for renewables prefer a law that would presumably create a freer market?

    AT: Well, those kind of claims are based on what are so-called comparisons of unsubsidized levelized costs of fresh electricity generation. That’s the standard measure. And outfits like Lazard have produced numbers that show, for instance, that onshore wind can be had for a cost of between $37 and $99 per megawatt hour, utility-scale solar for between $40 and $98, combined-cycle natural gas for $51 to $129, and so on and so forth.

    In a recent development, and when you make the comparisons on that basis, it’s generally true that solar and onshore wind come out as the optimum strategies. But they’re very, very partial measures of cost. Because what they don’t really account for is intermittency fundamentally. Right now, we really shouldn’t be making comparisons of just pure solar and wind versus gas because gas can be turned on and off once you’ve got the infrastructure. Whereas obviously solar and rain can’t. It depends on the availability of sunshine and wind. So they need to be backed up by batteries. Once you do the backup by batteries, they’re still competitive, but the argument is not as simple as saying that they’re the cheapest.

    But broadly speaking, I, in fact, entirely agree with the general thrust of your message. I’m an optimist on this question. And I think this is also the position, for instance, of the abundance agenda types, [Ezra] Klein and [Derek] Thompson and so on, which is that it’s a totally reasonable argument to make—namely that in the end, these technologies are superior. They are cheaper. People are investing in them. If you look in the pipeline, the pipeline is overwhelmingly renewables. And that’s not for reasons of wokeness. There are issues of intermittency, but the harder we push at this, the more we invest, the more the urgency will be to find solutions to them. And markets that are relatively free, like that of Texas, for instance, have turned out to be huge pioneers of rapid adoption of solar and wind. So I think, broadly speaking, that argument is well merited.

    Sources indicate that the risk is—and this is where somebody like a McKibben will come in—would be to say, well, that’s all very well, but at the margin, we can’t be certain that this game will play out necessarily in the favor of renewables. And the argument here is not coal anymore. Once upon a time, you might have stated coal could come back as a source of electricity generation. I think that argument is done everywhere outside China, probably. [There are] very few places in the world where coal makes any sense. Nuclear, for those who have environmental concerns about nuclear, [is] also prohibitively expensive. A free market option without subsidy probably kills it completely stone-dead given its costs. The real glitch is gas.

    Industry observers note that and the lesson here is not abstract—it’s historical. Because in the 2010s, what happened is that the entire calculus of the electricity-generating investment game in the United States was changed by the sudden availability of huge quantities of dirt-cheap shale gas, so fracked gas. And that had the effect of considerably displacing the adoption of wind and solar, which actually progressed more rapidly in Europe because gas prices—despite all of the talk of cheap gas from Russia, it was always nonsense. The really cheap gas comes from Texas, it comes from Pennsylvania, it comes from shale in the United States. And that considerably slowed down the adoption of more sustainable, more renewable energy sources. But broadly speaking, of course, it’s still a win. And folks from within the Obama administration embraced this under the heading of “all of the above” because gas replacing coal is a net win in terms of emissions. You might quibble with this if you think about the methane admitted in the production of gas, but nevertheless, it is a step in the right direction.

    Industry observers note that so the general thrust of your question, I think, should be affirmed. You know, we should not be thinking of renewables as a sort of endangered technology that needs protecting against the significant beasts of fossil industry. Are there fossil risks? Yes, but they come largely from innovation in the fossil sector and not the old enemies. Not coal, not nuclear—oil has never really been in the game here anyway for electricity generation, not since the ’70s. But that, to my mind, means that this should be weighed up in terms of exactly how much build-out of which types of energy we expect. It’s not a matter of principle that renewables should favor regulation, fossils should favor deregulation. It’s not as simple as that. It’s a conjunctural specific historical gamble that, in the current moment, the benefits outweigh the downsides.

    What we’re seeing, unfortunately, under Trump is that the biggest build-out and the biggest acceleration of electricity demand in American history—in recent times at least—probably ever in American history actually in terms of sheer volume, is taking place under an administration that seems determined to block renewables and under a permitting system that doesn’t permit a rapid build-out of efficient capacity. And the disaster there is it’s channeling all of that AI demand into gas-fired generation. It’s not epic by global standards; this isn’t China’s coal build-out. But it’s taking America in the wrong direction. And that’s the backdrop also against which this conversation is taking place right now. We see that there is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity or historic opportunity to have accelerated American electrification along green lines, and it’s being obstructed.

    Recent findings suggest that cameron Abadi is a deputy editor at Foreign Policy. X: @CameronAbadi.

    Adam Tooze is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a history professor and the director of the European Institute at Columbia University. He is the author of Chartbook, a newsletter on economics, geopolitics, and history. X: @adam_tooze.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • CHARLES KUPCHAN is Professor of International Affairs at Georgetown University and a Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.
    • President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin could be holding a three-way summit on the sidelines of next week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in Shenzhen, China.
    • These worries are entirely justified; Trump has a track record of cozying up to autocrats and turning his back on democratic allies.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    CHARLES KUPCHAN is Professor of International Affairs at Georgetown University and a Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. He is the author of Bringing Order to Anarchy: Governing the World to Come.

    In just a few days’ time, U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin could be holding a three-way summit on the sidelines of next week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in Shenzhen, China. According to The Wall Street Journal, Putin floated the idea of a trialogue last month as an opportunity to discuss ending the war in Ukraine. No firm plan has yet been declared, but even the prospect of this meeting has provoked widespread consternation. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski warned against a repeat of the Yalta Conference of 1945, when U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill capitulated to Soviet leader Joseph Stalin’s push for the Soviet Union to dominate Eastern Europe. U.S. Senator Chris Coons posted on X that “there can be no talks about Ukraine’s future without Ukraine at the table, and there can be no real negotiations as long as Trump signals weakness and servitude to Xi and Putin at every opportunity.”.

    These worries are entirely justified; Trump has a track record of cozying up to autocrats and turning his back on democratic allies. Should he sit down with Xi and Putin, he must avoid selling out European and Asian partners who will not be at the table. And given the three leaders’ headstrong personalities and competing national interests that pit the United States against what Xi calls a “no limits” partnership between China and Russia, the meeting might ultimately yield little progress on major challenges.

    Nevertheless, Trump would be right to join a summit with Xi and Putin. No U.S. president has ever held a trilateral meeting with the leaders of China and Russia, and the proposed talks would break the ice and begin to normalize much-needed dialogue. Authoritarianism is not going away, so autocracies and democracies must learn not only to live comfortably alongside one another but also to work together to tame geopolitical rivalry and tackle global challenges in an interdependent world. Americans will not find it easy to get along with the likes of Russia and China, whose political systems threaten the U.S. commitment to spreading democracy. But Trump is taking a bold step in the right direction by engaging with the heads of the world’s leading autocracies.

    If he meets with Xi and Putin, Trump should aim low and focus on making meaningful, if limited, progress on a small number of core challenges that could benefit from a three-way conversation: the flash points of the Korean Peninsula, Ukraine, and Iran, as well as arms control and strategic stability. But even if the summit yields no concrete results, it will nonetheless have been worthwhile. Trump, Xi, and Putin are paving the way for their successors to advance great-power cooperation across ideological lines and stabilize a fragmented world.

    I have argued previously, including in a 2021 Foreign Affairs essay with Richard Haass, that a global concert—an informal steering group of great powers modeled on the nineteenth-century Concert of Europe—offers the best hope of curbing geopolitical competition and enabling collective action in a multipolar world. In addition to the United States, China, and Russia, a new concert would include India, Japan, the European Union, and representatives from Africa, Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Concerts sacrifice representation for efficacy and give only the geopolitically influential states that must be there a seat at the table. They set aside ideological differences and bring democracies and autocracies together to focus on international cooperation. Because concerts eschew binding, enforceable procedures in favor of informal consensus building, they can succeed when formal institutions such as the UN Security Council are paralyzed and when the United States wavers in its commitment to rules-based multilateralism.

    In a recent development, but the time has not come for a global concert. Concerts function effectively only when their members are committed to the territorial status quo, are willing to exercise strategic restraint and pursue mutual benefits, and are ready to settle disputes diplomatically. Putin’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine and Xi’s decision to back Russia have, for now, scuttled hopes that the great powers will normalize restraint and the peaceful settlement of disputes. Meanwhile, Trump’s “America first” statecraft shuns joint action and mutual gain in favor of unilateralism.

    Yet even though Trump, Xi, and Putin are the wrong leaders at the wrong time to establish a great-power steering group that other major players would eventually join, Trump’s iconoclastic diplomacy sets a useful precedent. His Alaska summit with Putin last year and two summits with Xi this year were admittedly long on pageantry and short on substance. But by taking the controversial step of pursuing joint talks with the two leaders, Trump is widening the diplomatic Overton window and expanding what is politically possible for future U.S. presidents. Avoiding great-power conflict and taming a world in increasing disarray requires the United States to build constructive relations with both China and Russia. Trump deserves credit for starting a trialogue that his successors can carry forward.

    According to recent reports, if they meet in Shenzhen, Trump, Xi, and Putin should focus on easing tensions at key geopolitical flash points. The Korean Peninsula presents the best opportunity for the three leaders to collaborate. At the UN General Assembly in September, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung laid out an ambitious plan for normalizing relations with Pyongyang, including a proposal to replace the peninsula’s 1953 armistice with a “peace regime” that promotes “respect for each other’s systems and acknowledgement of our differences.” As part of that plan, Lee has advocated a phased approach to North Korean denuclearization, with an initial freeze on weapons development followed by gradual reductions in Pyongyang’s arsenal of nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles until the peninsula is denuclearized.

    According to recent reports, lee’s bold proposal could bring U.S., Chinese, and Russian interests into alignment. Trump has made it clear that he wants to de-escalate tensions on the Korean Peninsula and is already seeking a meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Beijing and Moscow are competing for influence over Kim, but both want a stable relationship between North and South Korea, so they might be willing to cooperate on proposals to halt nuclear weapons production and encourage talks between Pyongyang and Seoul. Trump, Xi, and Putin should aim to emerge from their meeting with a plan for advancing Lee’s peace agenda; jointly supporting a freeze on North Korean nuclear weapons development is a good place to start.

    The prospects for progress toward ending the war in Ukraine are much dimmer but not nonexistent. Trump should be striving to weaken Russia’s ability to sustain the war, but he has long resisted tightening sanctions on Moscow. He talks up potential business ventures with Russia and, in recent weeks, even struck a deal with Putin to get more Russian diesel into global markets and waived a new round of congressional sanctions against Moscow. Trump evidently cares more about trying to bring down fuel prices than about curbing Russia’s ability to fund its war against Ukraine.

    A summit offers Trump the opportunity to change course and try to convince Xi to restrain Putin. Trump has vowed to bring the war in Ukraine to an end, and the Chinese leader can help him achieve that goal. Xi has enormous leverage over Putin: China backs the Kremlin diplomatically, is the largest buyer of Russian oil and gas, and is the main supplier of dual-use items such as semiconductors and machine tools that are critical to Russian weapons manufacturing.

    It has been revealed that xi has played along with Putin’s war against Ukraine so far, presumably because the conflict diverts U.S. attention and resources away from Asia, divides NATO, and allows Xi and Putin to cast themselves as leading a global resistance to Western hegemony. But when Xi and Trump met this May, the leaders agreed to pursue “a constructive relationship of strategic stability” between China and the United States, which Xi could advance by pressing Putin to de-escalate. As more Russians feel the effects of the war, the Kremlin may be newly receptive to such pressure. Ukrainian drone strikes are taking a significant toll on Russia’s oil sector and logistics networks, which means Russian citizens face mounting gas and commodities shortages. Meanwhile, some 35,000 Russian soldiers per month are losing their lives or sustaining severe injuries in eastern Ukraine, forcing Putin to consider the unpopular move of ramping up military mobilization. With no battlefield victory in sight, Putin has reasons to entertain a diplomatic off-ramp.

    Trump and Xi could press Putin to accept a set of limited but consequential steps to de-escalate the conflict. These could include an agreement between Russia and Ukraine—brokered and monitored by Washington and Beijing—to end attacks on energy installations and infrastructure, civilian targets, and commercial shipping. Trump and Xi could also jointly press Putin to refrain from actions that could broaden the war, such as penetrating NATO airspace with Russian drones, sabotaging European infrastructure, and threatening to use nuclear weapons. This pressure, combined with the allure of improving diplomatic and commercial ties to the United States, might convince Putin to relent on at least some of these issues.

    Trump could also use a trilateral summit to seek help extricating the United States from its war in Iran—a quagmire that has produced regional mayhem and soaring oil prices. As Tehran continues to glitch maximalist demands and the war disrupts shipping through the straits of Hormuz and Bab el Mandeb, Trump needs an out.

    Neither Xi nor Putin has yet been inclined to lend a hand. China is still buying Iranian oil and providing Tehran with military intelligence and dual-use items that end up in Iranian drones and missiles, and Russia is providing satellite targeting data, munitions, advanced drone technology, and logistical support. Both Beijing and Moscow are happy to see the United States mired in a conflict that is exacerbating divisions within the American electorate and fracturing NATO.

    Sources indicate that as a major energy exporter, Russia benefits from the spike in oil prices that the conflict has triggered, so pressing Putin to cease supporting Iran is likely a lost cause. But China is the world’s largest oil importer, and Beijing has a vested interest in lowering energy prices by stabilizing exports from the Middle East. Although China’s large oil reserves have buffered its economy from rising oil prices so far, those reserves have been significantly depleted. China’s crude oil imports have begun to climb again, leaving its economy exposed to high energy prices if the conflict drags on. And as the world’s largest exporter of goods, China suffers from the dampening effect high energy prices have on global growth.

    It has been revealed that xi might therefore be amenable to helping Trump end the war. Trump should ask Xi to stop or at least slow the flow of Chinese dual-use items to Iran. Washington’s naval blockade and financial and commercial sanctions on Tehran have already taken a toll on Iran’s economy and military supply chains. By cutting off Chinese technology shipments to Iran, Beijing could deepen this economic isolation and help convince Tehran to negotiate an end to the conflict.

    Xi could also press Iran to drop its unrealistic demands for ending the war, including that the United States withdraw its forces from the Gulf, release frozen Iranian assets, and remove economic sanctions. Washington might well be willing to offer economic relief, but only as part of postwar negotiations toward a deal that reins in Iran’s nuclear ambitions. Xi could help clear the way for those talks by urging Iran to accept credible terms for ending the immediate conflict.

    Beyond working to resolve current conflicts, Trump should promote future strategic stability by pursuing arms control negotiations with Xi and Putin. Every arms control agreement negotiated between Washington and Moscow has expired; their final nuclear pact, Newly introduced START, ended in February. There are currently no caps on the American and Russian strategic arsenals and no regular inspections, data exchanges, or notifications of nuclear exercises. This nuclear free-for-all is particularly dangerous given Russia’s nuclear saber rattling amid the war in Ukraine and the Kremlin’s fondness for provocations such as sending explosive-laden drones into NATO airspace.

    In October, Trump appropriately proposed that a trilateral summit include a discussion of nuclear arms control. China has long resisted engaging in arms control talks, arguing that it should not have to limit its nuclear program when its arsenal is much smaller than that of the United States and Russia. But Beijing is rapidly expanding and modernizing its nuclear arsenal. The Pentagon has projected that China will possess more than 1,000 operational warheads by 2030, putting it in nearly the same league as the United States and Russia, which have stockpiles of roughly 1,800 operational warheads each. With the uncertain trajectory of U.S.-Chinese relations, instability on the Korean Peninsula, and China’s tense relationship with Taiwan heightening the risk of conflict in East Asia, Beijing must be part of high-level nuclear arms control discussions.

    Realistically, Trump can do little more than start this conversation and invite Xi and Putin to continue it in future trilateral negotiations led by teams of diplomats and arms control experts. In future talks, the three countries should discuss not only caps on nuclear weapons stockpiles but also military-to-military contacts, crisis management protocols, notifications of military exercises, counterproliferation, and other measures that can contribute to strategic stability.

    Trump could add a host of other topics to the summit’s agenda, including trade, energy security, and AI regulation, but he should avoid a wide-ranging conversation that goes nowhere. He might, however, notch an easy win by proposing a three-way initiative in an area in which cooperation is relatively straightforward—for example, a joint medical mission to the Democratic Republic of the Congo to help fight Ebola or a joint aid operation to deliver humanitarian relief to Gaza or Yemen. A concrete, public effort along these lines would show that trilateral dialogue can yield viable cooperation.

    According to recent reports, yet Trump should guard against being so eager for a win that he lets Xi and Putin take advantage of him. The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit takes place only two weeks after American voters dealt Trump and his party a historic rebuke in the U.S. midterm elections. The notoriously thin-skinned president could be tempted to make concessions to Beijing and Moscow to score a foreign policy breakthrough. He must avoid making a behind-closed-doors compromise on Ukraine that he then tries to force on Kyiv and its European supporters. Similarly, he must hold the line on Taiwan even as he seeks Xi’s help on North Korea, Ukraine, and Iran. Otherwise, Trump will leave the trilateral meeting confirming the worst fears of those who foresaw a latest Yalta in the making. Capitulating to Xi and Putin would alienate Washington’s allies, project American weakness, and erode global deterrence.

    Sources indicate that trump must also carefully manage the optics of a trilateral summit. Putin is an indicted war criminal who continues to prosecute a ruthless war of aggression against Ukraine. It is far too soon to let him out of the penalty box. And although Washington is right to seek a good working relationship with Beijing, it is time for Trump’s “truly great friendship” with Xi to bear fruit. Trump must approach talks with sobriety and pragmatism, seeking to demonstrate that Washington, Beijing, and Moscow can work together to help promote global peace and stability.

    A summit next week will not usher in a new era of great-power collaboration anytime soon. It might not even yield concrete deliverables. Still, the meeting would set a valuable precedent. Simply by sitting down with Xi and Putin, Trump would begin a much-needed trilateral conversation.

    Hail Mary effort on college sports bill could boost power conferences

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1114 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ted Cruz, R-Texas, pictured talking with reporters Nov.
    • President Donald Trump and GOP leaders are mounting a late push for a sweeping college sports bill that has stalled in the House, with newly introduced revisions that appear designed to appeal to several large state delegations by making it easier for high-profile schools to jump to the most lucrative conferences.
    • Sources indicate that the Senate’s version of the bill known as the Protect College Sports Act, which passed in September, would cap collegiate athletic conference sizes at 20 schools.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, pictured talking with reporters Nov. 17, has expressed confidence the Protect College Sports Act can clear Congress before the end of session. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    President Donald Trump and GOP leaders are mounting a late push for a sweeping college sports bill that has stalled in the House, with newly introduced revisions that appear designed to appeal to several large state delegations by making it easier for high-profile schools to jump to the most lucrative conferences.

    Sources indicate that the Senate’s version of the bill known as the Protect College Sports Act, which passed in September, would cap collegiate athletic conference sizes at 20 schools. But a revised House version released Friday evening would raise that conference roster cap to 22 institutions after several Atlantic Coast Conference schools went public with their collective desire for the change.

    The change could clear the way for another round of conference realignment, including the Southeastern Conference and Big Ten expanding again after both did so in 2024.

    College sports insiders have reported for some time that SEC and Substantial Ten officials have been eying a number of ACC schools to join their ranks — a list that includes the University of Florida, Florida State, the University of North Carolina and South Carolina’s Clemson University. All four recently sent letters to House lawmakers requesting the conference size change, according to the Charlotte Business Journal.

    The SEC and Big Ten currently have 16 members for revenue-generating sports.

    To reach the revised House bill’s 22-team ceiling, there has been speculation about other ACC schools also jumping ship, including North Carolina State University, Duke University, Wake Forest University, the University of Virginia and Virginia Tech. Because the bill, even with changes made by House Republican leaders, faces an uphill battle in the chamber, the 22-team cap change could assist its proponents.

    Sources indicate that that’s because of factions that have opposed college sports legislation. The nearly 60-member Congressional Black Caucus still opposes the measure over GOP efforts to terminate majority-minority House districts and an assessment it would not do enough to help historically Black colleges and universities. And some House conservatives have raised concerns that it might hurt colleges and conferences by allowing student athletes to do things like unionize.

    Industry observers note that the Sunshine, Tar Heel and Old Dominion states have 53 total House seats, making the conference cap change a potentially tactical weapon, should the amended measure hit the House floor. The House Rules Committee, in a Friday evening announcement, signaled the revised bill could get floor votes next week, after the chamber returns from a Thanksgiving recess.

    Sources indicate that the same Rules announcement informed members they have until midday Wednesday to submit further amendments ahead of a likely committee session on the legislation next week. If the panel signs off on a rule for the revised measure and some amendments, the next stop would be the chamber floor.

    The bill got a big boost from Trump during a Friday press conference at the White House.

    “If we don't pass that bill, you're not only going to not have sports, but you're going to have every college in the country go bankrupt,” Trump noted.

    A White House official signaled the president was not concerned about the proposed House changes. “The president wants NIL reform to get done and for Congress to send him a bill that can reach his desk quickly,” the official mentioned in an email.

    House Republicans did not make any changes to the Senate-passed measure’s provisions meant to help safeguard women’s sports.

    Recent findings suggest that house GOP leaders have proposed dropping the Senate’s threshold for when any conference merger would trigger antitrust violations. The House is proposing a breach of those laws if a conference that makes $600 million attempts to merge with or acquire another conference, down from the Senate’s $700 million level.

    Along with the proposed conference size and antitrust changes, the chamber’s revised bill would make a handful of targeted changes, including newly introduced rules for how colleges and universities count name, image and likeness (NIL) agreements against a revenue-share cap.

    According to recent reports, it also proposes changing schools’ disclosure requirements for student athletic fees and a lower threshold for certain conference mergers. And it proposes changes to what would be a new congressional commission to oversee the college athletics landscape.

    The House has proposed altering the Senate-passed bill’s NIL accounting language with a provision stating that any institution with annual average media rights revenue of at least $50 million could no longer use student fees to help finance their sports teams. The change appears geared toward lawmakers hailing from districts with HBCUs, smaller “Group of Six” FBS conference members and schools that compete in Football Championship Subdivision.

    The revised measure would stipulate that all NIL agreements between a student athlete and an institution, an institution employee or volunteer, a conference, a conference employee or an associated entity would count against that institution’s revenue-share cap and player-retention funds.

    In another proposed alteration, institutions of higher learning would be required to report certain student athlete compensation data “individually by program and in the aggregate.” The Senate-approved bill would have required reporting “for personnel of each intercollegiate sports program.”.

    Instead of allowing “a person” to bring a civil action, as would the Senate-approved language, the rewritten House provision would grant such rights only to a “current or former student athlete.”.

    The House version also would make several changes to the Senate’s proposed 24-member Congressional Commission on the Future of College Athletics by shaking up which congressional committees would get to select its members. The changes also include adding representation from midsized conferences and would give one seat to “a student athlete or former student athlete.”.

    In a brief interview last week, Senate Commerce Committee Chair Ted Cruz remarked he was confident the House would pass the bill “the week after Thanksgiving.”.

    Industry observers note that “There’s plenty of time,” the Texas Republican, a co-author of the Senate bill, said when asked if the lame-duck session’s remaining planned three weeks would allow the House to finish its work on the measure and then give the Senate time to vote on an amended version. The House is slated to leave for a holiday season recess on Dec. 17; the Senate is scheduled to exit the next day.

    “I believe the House is going to take it up and pass the bill,” Cruz said, adding that he had talked to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., about his looks. “I believe we will see in the House what we saw in the Senate: an overwhelming bipartisan vote.”.

    Breaking: After ‘Wild Horse Nine,’ 5 of the Best Movies About the CIA

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2169 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In Martin McDonagh’s upcoming film, Wild Horse Nine, there’s a moment where a younger CIA operative is trying to make his older comrade, who is dying of cancer and worried about his soul, feel better.
    • “You’re going to get to heaven, Chris,” Lee (Sam Rockwell) assures John Malkovich’s character.
    • In Martin McDonagh’s latest film, Wild Horse Nine, there’s a moment where a younger CIA operative is trying to make his older comrade, who is dying of cancer and worried about his soul, feel better.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    In Martin McDonagh’s upcoming film, Wild Horse Nine, there’s a moment where a younger CIA operative is trying to make his older comrade, who is dying of cancer and worried about his soul, feel better.

    “You’re going to get to heaven, Chris,” Lee (Sam Rockwell) assures John Malkovich’s character. “There’s whole countries that wouldn’t be free if not for you. Guatemala. Indonesia. That place in Africa I can never remember the name of. Sure you killed some people. So fucking what?” Do people who work at the CIA really talk this way? God, I hope not.

    In Martin McDonagh’s latest film, Wild Horse Nine, there’s a moment where a younger CIA operative is trying to make his older comrade, who is dying of cancer and worried about his soul, feel better.

    “You’re going to get to heaven, Chris,” Lee (Sam Rockwell) assures John Malkovich’s character. “There’s whole countries that wouldn’t be free if not for you. Guatemala. Indonesia. That place in Africa I can never remember the name of. Sure you killed some people. So fucking what?” Do people who work at the CIA really talk this way? God, I hope not.

    But then again, Wild Horse Nine, set during the 1973 Chilean coup, isn’t really about the CIA. The dark comedy—a good bet for landing several Academy Award nominations—is about mortality and remorse and how even the most brazen people can have moments of clarity and reevaluate their past actions. It uses the CIA as a skin, the way McDonagh’s previous (and very similar) fatalistic comedy In Bruges did with contract killers.

    Industry observers note that although its average employee likely has a job as mundane as any other government worker, an organization as key to world affairs and as necessarily shrouded in mystery as the CIA is understandably a great font for storytellers. But I can’t say there have been too many classic films that treat the CIA seriously.

    In a recent development, there have been some marvelous paranoid thrillers, specifically Watergate-era classics like Three Days of the Condor, which tend to get a little far-fetched by the third act. There are some exceptions, like 2005’s Syriana and 2014’s A Most Wanted Man, that show the minutiae of spy craft in a compelling way that doesn’t devolve into silliness. These are rarities. I also don’t really consider Sicario or Zero Dark Thirty CIA films, because their sweep covers multiple government agencies.

    Recent findings suggest that the lengthy 2006 film The Good Shepherd, directed by Robert De Niro and starring Matt Damon, was an attempt to show how the agency grew out of Yale secret societies and reached a crisis point during the Bay of Pigs. Despite some good intentions, though, the movie is a significant dud and has few champions. (I recently revisited the film, but found myself needing several attempts, after I fell asleep on the couch on more than one occasion.).

    Even for pure action-adventure absurdity, Britain has James Bond, but the United States has … James Bond’s friend Felix Leiter? Nice guy and all, but not 007. Mission: Impossible’s Ethan Hunt works for the Impossible Missions Force, remember, not the CIA. In the 1960s, Derek Flint, a Bond knockoff, worked for Z.O.W.I.E. (Zonal Organization World Intelligence Espionage), and Matt Helm worked for ICE (Intelligence and Counter-Espionage). Other than Jack Ryan, whose recent Amazon series and films have been absolutely horrible, Hollywood hasn’t given us a CIA man who’s become a household name.

    There have, of course, been great movies about the CIA, but all of them are laced with comedy. Maybe this is some kind of national defense mechanism? Hey, don’t mind us, we may be tinkering in the affairs of other sovereign nations, but we know it’s a little naughty.

    If the dark comedy of Wild Horse Nine has you itching for more examples of this curious phenomenon, here are five titles you can stream—all of which are intellectually zesty and a great deal of fun. (The Good Shepherd has value, too, should you find your stash of zolpidem depleted.) I’ve listed them from least-to-most zany.

    Bryan Cranston and Ben Affleck in Argo.IMDB.

    It has been revealed that this extremely watchable spy movie—with a healthy dose of comedy—was a major financial success and also won the Academy Award for best picture. (It beat both Steven Spielberg’s Lincoln and the aforementioned Zero Dark Thirty, both of which I’d place higher, but much like an operation to destabilize a country’s democracy, Oscar success isn’t always predictable.).

    In a recent development, the story is rooted in a true event: During the Iran hostage crisis, a CIA agent (Affleck) created an elaborate cover story to smuggle home six Americans who were hiding with the Canadian ambassador. His cockamamie blueprint was to fake being a Canadian film production that was scouting for locations. To make it work, there had to be a real script (a Star Wars knockoff) plus actual Hollywood producers and craftspeople—so Alan Arkin and John Goodman (playing John Chambers, the real-life guy who did the prosthetics for Planet of the Apes) join in.

    Sources indicate that naturally, there are setbacks and raised stakes as the baddies piece together which Americans are missing, then there’s a race against the clock for the major finish. Sadly (well, not for the real people involved), the action-adventure elements of the last act were made up for the movie. But Argo is still an engrossing heist-style picture. It has respect for the CIA, but also presents an agency with a prankster’s edge.

    Funnily enough, a 1966 crime-comedy from Italian director Vittorio De Sica and Upcoming York playwright Neil Simon called After the Fox used the idea of a fake movie production as the cover for a grand scheme—but in their case, it was smuggling gold.

    More recently, a group of Hollywood producers used the Argo technique as cover for an actual scheme in Poland, trying to recover a cache of stamps believed stolen from concentration camp prisoners. They even made a documentary film, The Stamp Thief, about the charade.

    It has been revealed that julia Roberts and Tom Hanks in Charlie Wilson’s War. IMDB.

    Sources indicate that in the months after 9/11, like many freaked-out Americans, I would stay up until dawn watching cable news stations, which is where I first learned the term “blowback,” and about how some felt that the CIA’s backing of the Mujahideen against the Soviets in Afghanistan caused a domino effect that eventually knocked down the Twin Towers. If I tried to explain what I’d seen the night before on C-SPAN 2, I sounded a bit like a paranoid lunatic, so I was very happy when screenwriter Aaron Sorkin and director Mike Nichols collaborated on Charlie Wilson’s War, a scathingly dark CIA satire that summed a lot of this up.

    The always affable Tom Hanks stars as the sleazy titular congressman who, from a Vegas hot tub filled with Playboy models, sees a 60 Minutes report about Afghan refugees. It’s 1980, and he’s worried about Soviet encroachment, but also finds himself (somewhat to his surprise) genuinely caring about civilians caught up in large geopolitical events.

    He finds likeminded spirits in Joanne Herring (Julia Roberts), a wealthy Houston socialite and political activist, and Gust Avrakotos (Philip Seymour Hoffman), a working-class CIA operative with a brilliant mind, well-honed bullshit detector, and extremely short temper who was just passed over for promotion. Like Argo, Charlie Wilson’s War is practically a heist picture, but about pushing levers in Washington to quietly appropriate funds and bring matériel to the Afghan fighters.

    The dark punchline, of course, is how our heroes are powerless when it comes time to “win the peace,” as it were, leaving a power vacuum that, it can easily be argued, was filled by al Qaeda. The film’s release at the end of George W. Bush’s presidency functioned as a needed release valve.

    Walter Matthau in Hopscotch.IMDB.

    Recent findings suggest that quite the opposite of seductive Sean-Connery-as-007 is hangdog Walter Matthau, but the dark comedy Hopscotch suggests they have some traits in common. Matthau plays Miles Kendig, a veteran CIA agent whose boss (Ned Beatty) takes him out of the field and sticks him with a desk job. As revenge, Kendig decides he’ll write his memoirs (much like Malkovich in Wild Horse Nine), and his spilled secrets make security agencies across the globe very nervous. As he sends salacious excerpts to international higher-ups from various international hiding spots, one of the few things the CIA and KGB can agree upon is: Get Matthau away from his typewriter!

    Aiding him is an old flame (Glenda Jackson, who also starred with Matthau’s in the popular comedy House Calls) who lives in Austria, which is a nice touch because our lead character is an opera nut who likes to sing along (poorly) to Mozart in the car.

    What Hopscotch has in common with Charlie Wilson’s War is presenting CIA bosses as absolute buffoons. The best part is when Matthau uses Beatty’s own vacation home as a hideout—which America’s intelligence forces then shoot to pieces. While Walter Matthau circa 1980 isn’t the most athletic secret agent, he’s quick with disguises, voices, thinking on his feet, and laying out elaborate traps. This is a great old school comedy with just enough post-Watergate negativity to keep it sharp.

    Alan Arkin and Peter Falk in The In-Laws.IMDB.

    Hopscotch is a little wacky. The In-Laws is full-on madcap. It’s also one of the funniest movies ever made, though its serpentine plot is hard to explain in just a few sentences. But I’ll give it a go….

    Alan Arkin plays a nervous dentist whose daughter is getting married to a nice kid, but Arkin hasn’t yet met the boy’s family. Turns out the father, played by Peter Falk, is a noisy madman who is either bank robber or a rogue CIA agent with blockhead bosses in the middle of an elaborate scheme to overthrow a Latin American dictator. Things soon spiral out of control, and this odd couple find themselves in several high-speed chases, dodging bullets while still hoping to make it to the wedding in time. The two great actors zing each other with quality barbs, and when that’s been exhausted there’s some physical comedy, too.

    The screenplay, written by Andrew Bergman, who also worked on Blazing Saddles, Fletch, and Soapdish, offers a much milder version of the impudence toward the CIA that you see in Wild Horse Nine. “You win some, you lose some,” Peter Falk shrugs when asked about the Bay of Pigs. Though this movie is mostly a comedic joy, the notion that U.S. intelligence is in the hands of nutcases at best—or sheer incompetents at worst—finds quick purchase here and seems to have reverberated in the decades since.

    Brad Pitt and Frances McDormand in Burn After Reading. IMDB.

    According to recent reports, there’s a lot about John Malkovich’s Wild Horse Nine character, Chris Carlisle, that may feel familiar. In Burn After Reading, the Coen brothers’ shaggiest movie (besides The Massive Lebowski), Malkovich plays Osborne Cox, a CIA agent who is demoted and decides to write a vicious memoir. But unlike the overlooked and pen-poised agents mentioned on this list already, Cox is a complete klutz.

    Sources indicate that but so is everyone in this tale, which includes Brad Pitt as dunderhead gym trainer Chad Feldheimer who, after a wild string of goof-ups and misunderstandings, ends up with a computer disc holding the first draft of Cox’s book. Feldheimer thinks he’s stumbled upon some serious material (it’s really just drunken grievances) and decides to blackmail Cox. This does not go well, and a ripple effect includes a murderer’s row of daffy performances from George Clooney, Frances McDormand, Richard Jenkins (more dumb than daffy), J.K. Simmons (exasperated by the stupidity around him, but powerless), and others.

    In a recent development, this was the Coen brothers’ follow-up to No Country For Old Men, their Oscar-winning crime drama based on Cormac McCarthy’s dark tale of greed and fate, and it’s probably the most cartoonish thing they’ve ever done. The CIA is nothing but a punching bag for 96 minutes, but the remaining undercurrent of violence erupts from time to time in some shocking (but hilarious) moments. Burn After Reading pushes the silliness to the absolute edge, but still somehow feels like parts of it could be true.

    Jordan Hoffman is a film critic and entertainment journalist living in central Upcoming Jersey. He also publishes at Vanity Fair, Entertainment Weekly, and the Times of Israel. He is a member of the New York Film Critics Circle and co-author of The Star Trek Book of Friendship. X: @jhoffman.
