    Latest Update: The World’s Last Chance for Peace

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3941 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.
    • At some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable.
    • Nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.

    At some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable. Wars of aggression, from Ukraine to Lebanon to Iran, are on the rise, bringing horror, ruin, and the specter of a wider international confrontation. Governments increasingly treat war as something to budget and prepare for. Military spending is climbing, technological and arms races are intensifying, and more and more countries are considering whether they should acquire a nuclear deterrent to guarantee their security.

    Nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war. It represents a return to a norm that persisted for most of human history, when war was the main organizing principle of the international system. Armed conflict was the natural way for states to settle disputes or enlarge their territory at the expense of weaker neighbors.

    Yet the vast wreckage of World Wars I and II in the first half of the twentieth century made the status quo unacceptable. Countries united behind an effort to turn war from a legitimate instrument of statecraft into an outlawed act. Wars did not end in 1945, but for years after they were overwhelmingly condemned by the international community.

    In recent decades, however, governments’ commitment to the cause of peace has weakened. Millions of people took to the streets in hundreds of cities to oppose the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, but the war proceeded nonetheless. Fought on false premises and in violation of international law, it brought destruction to Iraq, fed regional instability, and fueled resentment and terrorism directed at Western countries. The conflict also marked a turning point. Ever since, the pursuit of peace has steadily receded from the international agenda amid deepening geopolitical competition and inattention or indifference to the multilateral efforts that for decades discouraged acts of war.

    In a recent development, at the end of this path lies another world war—the catastrophe the twentieth-century order was designed to prevent. With that dire future looming, governments must relearn the art of opposing war. It is the responsibility of every country, including my own, Spain, to take direct action that constrains others’ ability to wage war and to strengthen the international institutions that will serve as guarantors of peace.

    The success of this project will depend on an expansive multilateralism that I call “maxilateralism”—cooperation that embraces as many countries as possible, rather than being limited to small, ad hoc groupings. Its ambition is to make war increasingly impractical, even unimaginable. In 2003, protesters across Spain chanted “No a la guerra!’’—“No to war!” The world cannot afford to ignore them again.

    Recent findings suggest that international efforts to reject war as an instrument of national policy date back to the Kellogg–Briand Pact of 1928, a treaty signed in Paris by 15 countries and joined by dozens more later. It was insufficient to prevent World War II, but it planted a seed. When representatives of 50 countries gathered in San Francisco in 1945 to create the United Nations, they revived the spirit and principles of Kellogg–Briand and gave them what they had lacked: institutional form. The UN Charter prohibited the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of another state. And, unlike its 1928 predecessor, it backed up the prohibition with institutions empowered to enforce it.

    In the decades that followed, these institutions established an order that penalized violations and created incentives for diplomacy and cooperation. At the same time, public opposition to war was growing stronger around the world. Popular defiance of Cold War militarism was visible in worldwide resistance to the Vietnam War and in mass movements against nuclear weapons. Pacifism reached its high-water mark in the 1990s, when a vibrant global civil society mobilized to defend humanitarian causes and when the United Nations held sufficient authority to champion a sweeping peace agenda.

    In a recent development, today, however, there is more armed conflict than at any time since 1946. According to the Uppsala Conflict Data Program, there were 65 active conflicts involving governments in 2025, double the number in 2010. An estimated 250,000 people died in those conflicts—the highest annual death toll in 30 years, since the Rwandan genocide. Close to 120 million people worldwide have been forcibly displaced by war.

    According to recent reports, worryingly, wars of aggression—which violate the UN Charter—are back. Russia invaded Ukraine. The United States and Israel attacked Iran. And as fighting continues year after year in places such as Lebanon, Sudan, and Yemen, it is becoming clear that war is being accepted as a normal occurrence.

    There is no sign of the trend slowing down. Military budgets have surged to levels not seen in generations, at the expense of social and development spending. In the past decade alone, global defense spending has increased by more than 40 percent, with many countries doubling their military budgets. The nearly $3 trillion the world spends annually on defense is close to the GDP of the entire African continent. Even countries with a long tradition of military restraint, such as Denmark, Germany, Japan, and Norway, are rearming rapidly. Some are reviving military service programs.

    It has been revealed that A renewed threat of nuclear war is cause for still greater dread. All nine nuclear-armed states are modernizing their arsenals, boosting their destructive capabilities. China’s nuclear arsenal is estimated to have increased from 200 to 300 warheads in the late 2010s to 620 this year. North Korea has also expanded its arsenal from an estimated ten to 20 warheads in 2018 to around 60 this year, and it has developed increasingly sophisticated launch platforms. In March, France declared the first increase in its nuclear warhead stockpile since 1992. The United States and Russia, the world’s two largest nuclear powers, have failed to preserve the last remaining treaty constraining their strategic arsenals. And a growing number of nonnuclear powers have started to consider acquiring arsenals of their own.

    It has been revealed that simultaneously, artificial intelligence is powering ever more dangerous weapons of war. Human oversight is being progressively reduced as AI makes it possible to automate cyberattacks against power grids, hospitals, and financial systems. AI systems have hacked government bodies and enabled the mass production of deepfakes and disinformation campaigns.

    In a recent development, the integration of AI into nuclear technologies poses an existential threat: as AI speeds up decision-making, it reduces the time available for human judgment. Similarly, the use of AI in biotechnology could dramatically lower barriers to harmful experimentation and the development of bioweapons. In both areas, this technology is elevating the risk of miscalculation, unintended escalation, and mass destruction to a level higher than ever before.

    Together, these dynamics are multiplying the chances that any crisis will promptly spiral into planetary annihilation. Countries are building the instruments of catastrophe at the blinding speed of innovation while the instruments of control move at the much slower pace of diplomacy.

    Political change is pushing the world away from peace and toward confrontation and militarization. A multipolar world is not, by definition, a more dangerous one, but the erosion of rules and institutions that manage tensions between poles has made today’s world particularly volatile. Competition among great powers is increasing, with hegemonic ambitions encouraging assertive foreign policies and revisionist states challenging established rules and borders. Belligerent nationalism is on the rise, and far-right movements are advancing a worldview in which international relations is a zero-sum game and countries must compete rather than cooperate. Even centrist leaders are embracing the language of war preparedness. Although they do not intend to start a war, their words feed a dangerous militaristic mindset.

    According to recent reports, in this context of rivalry, wars of aggression come wrapped in narratives of necessity, liberation, self-defense, or historical justice. The attackers present their operations as inevitable, having demonized their targets to justify preemptive action against them. They describe each war as an answer to insecurity—a war to end all wars.

    But these wars will not make a safer world. Every time a state embarks on a war of aggression, it erodes the norms that protect all countries from the arbitrary use of force—including the aggressor itself.

    Wars exact immense costs. They shatter societies and interrupt lives. In 2025, at least one civilian died in an armed conflict every 14 minutes, according to UN records, and more than five million people were forced to flee their countries. The economic costs are high, too; the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran has severely disrupted maritime trade and air traffic, driving up the prices of energy, fertilizer, and other commodities, and millions of people across the world are suffering the consequences.

    War also creates fresh dangers. Once the fighting begins, its course is unpredictable. Conflict tends to draw in new actors and spill into neighboring countries. The war in Iran serves, again, as a prime example. Since February 2026, Iran has struck targets in several Gulf countries and other neighbors—actions Spain has consistently condemned. Attacks on civilian and commercial vessels threaten broader regional stability. And the war has reignited conflicts in Iraq, Lebanon, and Yemen.

    Finally, wars rarely produce lasting peace. Instead, they deepen grievances and entrench divisions that fuel future violence. Russia’s war in Ukraine, for instance, has destroyed trust in Moscow. The genocide in Gaza has inflamed anger toward Israel, potentially leading to latest waves of terrorism. And the war against Iran has further destabilized the Middle East, hindering cooperation across the region.

    Recent findings suggest that the world has a responsibility to resist the normalization of wars. Remaining silent is an act of cowardice and complicity. Spanish society is making its position clear: three of four Spaniards identify war as their greatest fear, and an even greater number believe another world war is on the horizon.

    But it is not enough to simply condemn war in principle. The ambition of ending war must be matched with action that makes it increasingly difficult for countries to start, sustain, and justify armed conflict.

    Sources indicate that spain has endeavored to take such action. It has defended the international laws that stand between an order governed by rules and one governed by force. Spain has consistently denounced armed attacks that violate the UN Charter.

    From day one of the war in Gaza, Spain has been calling for an immediate and permanent cease-fire, the release of all hostages, and the unrestricted delivery of humanitarian assistance. In May 2024, Spain recognized the state of Palestine in the hope that this step would help advance a negotiated and lasting solution to the conflict. And Spain has actively supported the efforts of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court to hold Israeli leaders accountable for violations of international humanitarian law. Israel had the right to self-defense after the October 7 terrorist attacks, but that right does not justify genocide in Gaza or the expansion of Israel’s illegal occupation of the West Bank.

    It has been revealed that deterring war also requires raising the costs of aggression. The rest of the world must ensure that those who choose to wage war cannot do so without paying a price. Throughout Russia’s war in Ukraine, for example, the European Union has introduced a series of sanctions on Russia, which Spain has consistently supported. Spain has also provided financial, humanitarian, and military assistance to Ukraine, helping it defend its territory and deny Russia the spoils of war.

    Countries must refuse to help belligerents expand existing conflicts. Spain, for instance, has maintained an arms embargo on Israel since 2023. This year, it also denied the United States the use of its territory and facilities for the war against Iran. Spain’s decision was not an act of hostility toward an ally. Nor was it an expression of neutrality or sympathy for the Iranian regime. It was, rather, a judgment that getting involved would enable escalation of the conflict, deepening regional and global insecurity. To keep its commitment to peace, Spain had to be willing to say no, even when doing so carried a political cost. Had more countries done the same, the wars in Gaza and Iran would have been far harder and costlier to wage.

    According to recent reports, investing in prosperity is also essential. Security is strengthened when societies are resilient, inequalities are reduced, and citizens can rely on public institutions. Spain’s decision last year to opt out of NATO’s proposed defense spending target of five percent of GDP reflected this understanding. This position did not stem from a lack of commitment to European defense—in fact, my government has championed Europe’s push for strategic autonomy and has tripled net defense spending over the eight years I have been in office. But military deterrence and social welfare must reinforce each other. By keeping defense spending proportionate, Spain has preserved the fiscal space to invest an additional 145 billion euros in social protection, housing, health care, and education, as well as more than 30 billion euros in the green transition—programs that make society more cohesive and adaptable, and therefore more secure.

    Yet one country’s efforts can accomplish only so much. Starving war of its lifelines requires all hands on deck, a collective effort rooted in genuine multilateralism. This is the only strategy that has worked before. The multilateral system built after World War II spanned the globe, and it helped keep peace among great powers and prevent a third world war.

    Recent findings suggest that reinforcing it will not be an easy task. Geopolitical competition and widespread mistrust have weakened the United Nations, international financial bodies, regional organizations, and other multilateral institutions. Many countries perceive them as ineffective and trapped in perpetual crisis, so they have turned to alternative frameworks to try to end wars.

    Some have tried unilateral approaches, pursuing transactional bargains that end up benefiting economic and political elites while sidelining the populations affected by the conflict. The cease-fires or peace deals they achieve may be preferable to continued war, but any peace imposed through power politics rather than law rests on shaky foundations.

    According to recent reports, other countries, frustrated with multilateralism, have tried recruiting coalitions of the willing, or other “minilateral” groups, to provide security guarantees or reach ad hoc arrangements on matters of trade and technology. This approach might be a temporary solution to the paralysis of traditional institutions, but its exclusivity further fragments an already divided international order. What is needed is not minilateralism but maxilateralism. International cooperation is powerful when it is, or aspires to be, universal. Leaving part of the world outside of multilateral efforts, moreover, is a recipe for confrontation down the road.

    The twentieth-century system was not perfect. The application of its rules has been uneven, its standards inconsistently upheld, its procedures frustratingly slow. But it is undeniable that the world would be much more dangerous without it. To take just one example, it was a lattice of international treaties—including the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, and the Limited Test Ban Treaty—that ended a wildly expensive arms race that was driving the world to the brink of nuclear war.

    It has been revealed that all of this institutional architecture is now eroding. Yet without it, the world cannot aspire to preserve peace.

    Strengthening multilateral institutions must be at the center of a global campaign to relegate war to history. This will require substantial reform to restore these institutions’ legitimacy and their capacity to act, prioritizing measures that will contribute the most to peace and security.

    Recent findings suggest that the first is increasing representation at the United Nations and the Bretton Woods institutions. An upgrade to the structure of the UN Security Council is particularly vital, given that body’s primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace. A Security Council that gives permanent seats and a right to veto only to the five victors of World War II, which together account for barely a quarter of the global population, does not reflect today’s world. The council’s elected membership should be expanded and the terms of those members should be extended beyond the current two years. The newly introduced seats should be given primarily to countries in underrepresented regions, particularly Africa and Latin America. Regional organizations such as the European Union and the African Union should also be represented in the council, potentially taking over seats presently occupied by states. A more representative Security Council would not merely be fairer; it would also be more effective. Countries are more likely to defend and enforce international rules when they consider themselves to be authors of those rules.

    It has been revealed that permanent members’ veto power must also be strictly limited, particularly when the Security Council considers cases of mass atrocities, genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes. Ultimately, the veto should be abolished outright. Only then can the council respond to all acts of aggression without being paralyzed by the objections of a single state.

    Sources indicate that A similar spirit should guide structural change at international financial institutions, particularly the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. The distribution of voting power in both still reflects twentieth-century economic balances, and by convention, a European always leads the IMF and an American leads the World Bank. This must end. Emerging economies need better representation, and leadership positions should be open to all candidates regardless of nationality. Responsibilities within institutions such as the World Trade Organization should also evolve as economic growth moves countries that were once categorized as “developing” into the ranks of the wealthy. Fairer economic governance would ease the inequality and resentment that so often feed instability and conflict.

    Another key reform will involve reinvigorating the international framework that limits the risk of nuclear escalation. Some of that work depends on the nuclear powers; it is up to the United States and Russia, for example, to negotiate a successor to the bilateral New START treaty that preserves verifiable limits on strategic nuclear deployments. And this time, China should be part of the discussions.

    Sources indicate that yet the broader effort requires the engagement of all countries. Their priorities should include ratifying the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty to prevent a resumption of nuclear testing and advancing negotiations on a Fissile Material Cutoff Treaty, which would ban production of highly enriched uranium and plutonium for nuclear weapons. All countries must also work together to regulate the use of AI in the military domain, especially when it comes to nuclear weapons, to preserve human control over launch decisions and reduce the risk of catastrophic errors. Nonnuclear powers should commit to not acquiring nuclear weapons themselves, and they should use every tool at their disposal to encourage nuclear powers to reduce their arsenals, strengthen verification mechanisms, and rebuild the diplomatic guardrails that for decades have helped prevent nuclear catastrophe.

    Technology can help with some of this. Advances in satellite imagery, remote sensors, and data analytics can increase transparency and make compliance with arms control agreements more observable. But more must be done to avoid situations that can escalate into war. If nuclear-armed states agree to lower operational readiness and strengthen crisis communication, that can help ensure that governments have the time and the means to defuse dangerous situations. Each country must protect its command-and-control systems from cyberattacks and AI-driven manipulation of information, so that a false alarm or miscalculation never leads to nuclear war.

    Sources indicate that the final priority is to ensure that the international justice system can enforce courts’ decisions. Dismantling the International Criminal Court, as some countries are trying to do, would only ensure that the world’s gravest crimes go unpunished. The ICC should not only prosecute cases of genocide, aggression, war crimes, and crimes against humanity but also have the authority to bring to justice those who are responsible for these crimes. When a state becomes a party to the Rome Statute, the treaty that created the ICC, it agrees to submit itself to the court’s jurisdiction. Yet if that state refuses to cooperate or surrender a suspect, there is no real punishment, only an embarrassing censure. This must change. States that shelter individuals indicted by the ICC should face legal, diplomatic, and financial consequences. Starting and waging war should carry a real cost.

    Proposals to reform international institutions have long struggled to gain traction, but the coming election of a latest UN secretary-general offers a rare opportunity to inject fresh momentum into these efforts. Were the UN to appoint its first female leader, it would be a powerful symbol of renewal, inclusion, and institutional adaptation. The organization cannot truly claim to speak on behalf of all humanity until it has had a woman leading it. Reaching this milestone could kindle a new sense of ambition and instill greater confidence in the capacity of international institutions to reform themselves—and to reclaim their role in constraining war.

    Halting the world’s march toward war will require the broadest possible commitment. All countries, large and small, must refuse to look away or to participate in escalatory action. They must stand by the international norms that constrain war today, and reform and empower the institutions that will make it impossible tomorrow.

    Ultimately, what will make war unimaginable is a positive peace agenda that addresses the root causes of insecurity. Every step toward eradicating poverty, expanding access to quality education, advancing gender equality, strengthening democratic institutions, and increasing disaster resilience also eases the conditions that produce violence.

    According to recent reports, international financial institutions must be able to deliver financing swiftly, at scale, and at reasonable cost, so that no developing country is forced to choose between servicing its debt and investing in its people. Multilateral development banks must be able to mobilize funds for the green and digital transitions, so that climate migration and competition over resources do not become drivers of interstate conflict. And the World Health Organization’s Pandemic Agreement must be finalized and put into force to ensure that all countries will be able to access vaccines and treatments when the next global health emergency strikes.

    This is why Spain has sought to place development at the heart of its foreign policy. The Spanish government has championed the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals for 2030, and last year the city of Seville hosted the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, where delegates committed to easing the debt burden of vulnerable countries and unlocking investment for sustainable development. Spain has also promoted initiatives such as the Global Hub on Debt for Development Swaps, launched with the World Bank; the multilateral Debt Suspension Clause Alliance, which allows vulnerable countries to pause debt payments after disasters; and its own mechanism to provide up to 60 million euros in debt relief for developing countries each year. In addition, Spain has backed climate finance, global health, gender equality, food security, and social protection initiatives in partnership with multilateral institutions and international organizations. These development policies are peacebuilding policies, too.

    A larger project to rally the world behind legal norms and genuine multilateralism may seem unrealistic. But we have seen what happens when the normalization of war drags humanity into hell. The men and women who emerged from the ruins of World War II, the darkest chapter in human history, found a way to construct a multilateral world order. The question before our generation is whether we will preserve the rule of law or allow a return to rule by force. Whether we build the world of tomorrow through foresight and cooperation, or through the chaos and pain of another world war. We must choose wisely while the choice is still ours to make.

    What in the World?

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Have feedback? Email [email protected] to let me know your thoughts.

    In a recent development, 1. Which group kicked off its leaders’ summit in Manila, Philippines, on Sunday?

    4. On Tuesday, the Pan American Health Organization announced that Bolivia, Mexico, and the United States had lost their designation of having eliminated which disease?

    A measles outbreak has also been worsening in recent months in Bangladesh, which recorded around 200,000 suspected cases between mid-March and early October, FP’s Michael Kugelman wrote in South Asia Brief in October.

    Recent findings suggest that 5. On Wednesday, Iranian forces targeted a U.S. air base located in which country?

    The tit-for-tat strikes between Iran and the United States this week marked an end to a roughly two-month lull in such attacks, FP’s John Haltiwanger and Rishi Iyengar write in Situation Report.

    According to recent reports, 6. The United States signed a military partnership agreement with which Latin American country on Wednesday?

    In a recent development, U.S. officials said the deal was intended to help the two governments battle drug traffickers, but analysts believe that it could also be an opportunity for Washington to rein in the power of the Venezuelan military, FP’s Catherine Osborn reports in Latin America Brief.

    Recent findings suggest that 7. On Thursday, the International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya people. Which country brought the case before the court?

    This is the first time the court has found a state directly responsible for genocide, and it’s likely to have major implications for future cases, Andrew Nachemson writes.

    According to recent reports, 8. U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin held their first-ever trilateral meeting on Thursday. In which city did it take place?

    The meeting was no Yalta Conference, but it did provide the leaders with plenty of attention and a few photo ops, FP’s James Palmer writes in China Brief.

    9. Also on Thursday, Somalia expelled the ambassador of which country?

    The decision was partly prompted by Abu Dhabi’s relationship with several Somalian regions, including the breakaway province of Somaliland—whose quest for international recognition has been picking up steam, Joshua Keating wrote in September.

    Sources indicate that 10. On Wednesday, which spacecraft became the first human-made object to reach a distance of one light-day away from Earth?

    The European Space Agency’s Hera.

    Voyager 1 has now traveled more than four times the distance from the sun to Pluto—and as of next September, it will have been in space for 50 years, Smithsonian magazine reports.

    #156862. Industry News: La última oportunidad para la paz

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 23m • 📚 Deep Dive (4567 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: La última oportunidad para la paz

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • PEDRO SÁNCHEZ es presidente del Gobierno de España.
    • In a recent development, en algún momento de la última década, el mundo empezó a aceptar la guerra como algo inevitable.
    • According to recent reports, no hay nada más peligroso que normalizar la guerra.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    PEDRO SÁNCHEZ es presidente del Gobierno de España.

    Cómo evitar otra guerra mundial.

    In a recent development, en algún momento de la última década, el mundo empezó a aceptar la guerra como algo inevitable. Las guerras de agresión, como las de Ucrania, el Líbano o Irán, aumentan y siembran horror, ruina y el temor a una confrontación global. Los gobiernos piensan cada vez más en la guerra como algo para lo que hay que prepararse y presupuestar. El gasto militar no deja de crecer, las carreras tecnológicas y armamentísticas se intensifican, y cada vez más países se plantean si deberían dotarse de un arsenal nuclear disuasorio que garantice su seguridad.

    According to recent reports, no hay nada más peligroso que normalizar la guerra. Supone regresar a una norma que imperó durante la mayor parte de la historia de la humanidad. La guerra era el eje vertebrador del sistema internacional. Era la vía natural por la que los Estados zanjaban sus disputas o ensanchaban su territorio a costa de vecinos más débiles.

    Pero la inmensa devastación que produjeron las dos guerras mundiales en la primera mitad del siglo XX hizo inaceptable ese statu quo. Los países se unieron en un empeño común: que la guerra dejara de ser un instrumento legítimo de la política de Estado y pasara a ser un acto ilegal. Las guerras no terminaron en 1945, pero durante años la comunidad internacional las condenó de forma abrumadora.

    En las últimas décadas, sin embargo, el compromiso de los gobiernos con la causa de la paz se ha debilitado. En 2003, millones de personas salieron a las calles en cientos de ciudades para oponerse a la invasión de Irak liderada por Estados Unidos. Y, aun así, la guerra siguió adelante. Iniciada a partir de premisas falsas y en violación del derecho internacional, arrasó Irak, agravó la inestabilidad regional y avivó el resentimiento y el terrorismo contra los países occidentales. Aquel conflicto marcó, además, un punto de inflexión. Desde entonces, la búsqueda de la paz ha ido retrocediendo en la agenda internacional, arrinconada por la creciente competencia geopolítica y la desatención o la indiferencia hacia los esfuerzos multilaterales que durante décadas pusieron freno a la guerra.

    Recent findings suggest that este camino conduce a una nueva guerra mundial: la catástrofe que el orden del siglo XX se propuso evitar. Ante ese futuro sombrío en el horizonte, los gobiernos deben reaprender el arte de oponerse a la guerra. Todos los países, incluido el mío, España, tienen la responsabilidad de actuar para limitar la capacidad de otros de librar la guerra y para fortalecer las instituciones internacionales que han de ser garantes de la paz.

    El éxito de este proyecto dependerá de un multilateralismo expansivo, al que yo llamo «maxilateralismo»: una cooperación que abarque al mayor número posible de países, en lugar de limitarse a pequeñas coaliciones ad hoc. Su ambición es que la guerra resulte cada vez más inviable, incluso inimaginable. En 2003, manifestantes por toda España coreaban «¡No a la guerra!». En 2026, el mundo no puede volver a ignorarlos.

    Los esfuerzos internacionales por desterrar la guerra como instrumento de política nacional se remontan al Pacto Briand-Kellogg de 1928, un tratado firmado en París por 15 países, al que posteriormente se sumaron decenas más. No bastó para impedir la Segunda Guerra Mundial, pero plantó una semilla. Cuando representantes de 50 países se reunieron en San Francisco en 1945 para crear las Naciones Unidas, recuperaron el espíritu y los principios del Pacto y añadieron lo que había faltado: estructura institucional. La Carta de Naciones Unidas prohibió recurrir a la amenaza o al uso de la fuerza contra la integridad territorial o la independencia política de otro Estado. Y, a diferencia de su predecesor de 1928, respaldó esa prohibición con instituciones facultadas para hacerla cumplir.

    It has been revealed that en las décadas siguientes, estas instituciones levantaron un orden que castigaba las violaciones al derecho internacional e incentivaba la cooperación y la diplomacia. Al mismo tiempo, el rechazo popular a la guerra y al militarismo de la Guerra Fría cobraba fuerza en todo el mundo. Se hizo visible en la resistencia a la guerra de Vietnam y en los movimientos de masas contra las armas nucleares. El pacifismo alcanzó su punto álgido en los años noventa, cuando una sociedad civil global pujante se movilizó en defensa de causas humanitarias y Naciones Unidas tenía autoridad para abanderar una ambiciosa agenda de paz.

    Recent findings suggest that hoy, sin embargo, hay más conflictos armados que en ningún otro momento desde 1946. Según el Programa de Datos sobre Conflictos de Uppsala, en 2025 hubo 65 conflictos activos con participación estatal, el doble que en 2010. Se calcula que en estos conflictos murieron 250.000 personas: la cifra anual más alta desde el genocidio de Ruanda hace más de 30 años. Cerca de 120 millones de personas en todo el mundo siguen desplazadas por la guerra.

    Sources indicate that Y lo más inquietante: las guerras de agresión, que violan la Carta de Naciones Unidas, están de vuelta. Rusia invadió Ucrania. Estados Unidos e Israel atacaron Irán. Y mientras los combates se prolongan año tras año en lugares como el Líbano, Sudán o Yemen, resulta evidente que la guerra está siendo aceptada de nuevo como algo normal.

    Recent findings suggest that nada indica que esta tendencia vaya a frenarse. Los presupuestos militares se han disparado hasta niveles no vistos en generaciones, en detrimento del gasto social y de desarrollo. Solo en la última década, el gasto mundial en defensa ha aumentado más de un 40 %, y muchos países han duplicado sus presupuestos militares. Los casi 3 billones de dólares que el mundo destina cada año a defensa se acercan al producto interior bruto de todo el continente africano. Incluso países con una larga tradición de contención militar, como Alemania, Dinamarca, Japón y Noruega, se están rearmando a toda velocidad, y algunos están recuperando el servicio militar.

    It has been revealed that aún más estremecedor es el regreso de la amenaza de guerra nuclear. Los nueve Estados con armas nucleares están modernizando sus arsenales y aumentando su capacidad destructiva. Se calcula que el arsenal de China ha pasado de entre unas 200-300 cabezas nucleares a finales de la década de 2010 a 620 este año. Corea del Norte también ha ampliado el suyo, de entre 10-20 cabezas estimadas en 2018 a unas 60 este año, y ha desarrollado plataformas de lanzamiento cada vez más sofisticadas. En marzo, Francia anunció el primer aumento de su número de cabezas nucleares desde 1992. Estados Unidos y Rusia, las dos mayores potencias nucleares del mundo, no han sido capaces de preservar el último tratado que ponía límites a sus arsenales estratégicos. Y cada vez más potencias no nucleares han empezado a plantearse adquirir armas nucleares propias.

    Al mismo tiempo, la inteligencia artificial (IA) está dotando a la guerra de armas cada vez más peligrosas. La supervisión humana se reduce progresivamente a medida que la IA permite automatizar ciberataques contra redes eléctricas, hospitales y sistemas financieros. Hay sistemas de IA que ya han logrado infiltrarse en organismos públicos y han hecho posible la producción masiva de deepfakes y de campañas de desinformación.

    Industry observers note that la integración de la IA en las tecnologías nucleares es una amenaza existencial: al acelerar la toma de decisiones, comprime el tiempo disponible para el juicio humano. Del mismo modo, el uso de la IA en biotecnología podría rebajar drásticamente las barreras a la experimentación nociva y al desarrollo de armas biológicas. En ambos terrenos, esta tecnología está elevando a niveles sin precedentes el riesgo de errores de cálculo, de escaladas involuntarias y de destrucción masiva.

    En conjunto, estas dinámicas multiplican las probabilidades de que cualquier crisis desemboque rápidamente en la aniquilación del planeta. Por desgracia, los países están fabricando los instrumentos de la catástrofe a la velocidad vertiginosa de la innovación, mientras que los instrumentos de control avanzan al ritmo, mucho más lento, de la diplomacia.

    Industry observers note that los cambios políticos están alejando al mundo de la paz. Lo empujan hacia la militarización y la confrontación. Un mundo multipolar no es, por definición, más peligroso. Pero la erosión de las normas y de las instituciones que deberían encauzar las tensiones entre los distintos polos está provocando que el mundo se vuelva especialmente volátil. La competencia entre grandes potencias se intensifica: las ansias de hegemonía alientan políticas exteriores agresivas y los Estados revisionistas desafían las normas y las fronteras establecidas. El nacionalismo beligerante crece. Los movimientos de extrema derecha promueven una visión del mundo en la que las relaciones internacionales son un juego de suma cero y los países deben competir en lugar de cooperar. Incluso dirigentes de centro están adoptando la retórica de la guerra. Aunque no pretendan iniciar una, sus palabras abonan una mentalidad militarista peligrosa.

    En este clima de rivalidad, las guerras de agresión se envuelven en discursos de necesidad, liberación, legítima defensa o justicia histórica. Los agresores presentan sus operaciones como inevitables, después de haber demonizado a sus adversarios para justificar un ataque preventivo. Venden cada guerra como la respuesta a la inseguridad: la guerra que acabará con todas las guerras.

    In a recent development, pero estas guerras no harán del mundo un lugar más seguro. Cada vez que un Estado desata una guerra de agresión, erosiona las normas que protegen a todos los países frente al uso arbitrario de la fuerza, incluido el propio Estado agresor.

    Sources indicate that las guerras tienen un coste inmenso. Destrozan sociedades y truncan vidas. En 2025, según los registros de Naciones Unidas, al menos un civil murió en conflicto armado cada 14 minutos, y más de cinco millones de personas se vieron obligadas a huir de sus países. El coste económico también es altísimo. La guerra que enfrenta a Estados Unidos e Israel con Irán ha alterado gravemente el comercio marítimo y el tráfico aéreo y ha disparado los precios de la energía, los fertilizantes y otras materias primas. Millones de personas en todo el mundo están sufriendo las consecuencias.

    La guerra genera, además, nuevos peligros. Una vez que empiezan los combates, su rumbo es imprevisible. Los conflictos tienden a arrastrar a nuevos actores y a desbordarse hacia los países vecinos. La guerra de Irán vuelve a ser un ejemplo claro. Desde febrero de 2026, Irán ha atacado objetivos en varios países del Golfo y de su entorno, acciones que España ha condenado sin excepción. Los ataques contra buques civiles y mercantes amenazan la estabilidad del conjunto de la región. Y la guerra ha reavivado los conflictos de Irak, el Líbano y Yemen.

    Industry observers note that por último, las guerras rara vez traen una paz duradera. Al contrario: ahondan los agravios y enquistan las divisiones que alimentan la violencia del mañana. La guerra de Rusia en Ucrania, por ejemplo, ha dinamitado la confianza en Moscú. El genocidio en Gaza ha exacerbado la indignación contra Israel, y eso podría desembocar en nuevas oleadas de terrorismo. Y la guerra contra Irán ha desestabilizado aún más la región y ha lastrado la cooperación entre sus países.

    In a recent development, el mundo tiene la responsabilidad de resistirse a la normalización de la guerra. Callar es un acto de cobardía y de complicidad. La sociedad española está dejando clara su posición: tres de cada cuatro españoles señalan la guerra como su mayor temor. Y un número aún mayor cree que se cierne otra guerra mundial.

    According to recent reports, pero no basta con condenar la guerra en abstracto. La ambición de acabar con ella debe ir acompañada de acciones concretas que hagan cada vez más difícil que los países inicien, sostengan y justifiquen un conflicto armado.

    In a recent development, españa ha procurado actuar en esa dirección. Ha defendido las normas internacionales que marcan la diferencia entre un orden basado en reglas y otro gobernado por la fuerza. Y ha denunciado siempre los ataques armados que violan la Carta de Naciones Unidas.

    Desde el primer día de la guerra en Gaza, España ha reclamado un alto el fuego inmediato y permanente, la liberación de todos los rehenes y la entrada sin restricciones de la ayuda humanitaria. En mayo de 2024, España reconoció el Estado de Palestina con la esperanza de que este paso contribuyera a avanzar hacia una solución negociada y duradera del conflicto. Y ha apoyado activamente los esfuerzos de la Corte Internacional de Justicia y de la Corte Penal Internacional para que los dirigentes israelíes rindan cuentas por sus violaciones del derecho internacional humanitario. Israel tenía derecho a la legítima defensa tras los atentados terroristas del 7 de octubre. Pero ese derecho no justifica el genocidio en Gaza ni la expansión de la ocupación ilegal de Cisjordania.

    Disuadir la guerra exige también elevar el coste de la agresión. El resto del mundo debe asegurarse de que quien elija hacer la guerra no pueda hacerlo sin pagar un precio. A lo largo de la invasión rusa de Ucrania, por ejemplo, la Unión Europea ha aprobado sucesivas rondas de sanciones contra Rusia que España ha respaldado sin titubeos. España también ha prestado a Ucrania ayuda financiera, humanitaria y militar para que pueda defender su territorio y negarle a Rusia el botín de guerra.

    Recent findings suggest that los países deben negarse a ayudar a las partes a extender los conflictos en curso. España, por ejemplo, mantiene un embargo de armas a Israel desde 2023. Este año, además, negó a Estados Unidos el uso de su territorio y de sus instalaciones para la guerra contra Irán. La decisión de España no fue un acto de hostilidad hacia un aliado. Tampoco fue una expresión de neutralidad ni de simpatía hacia el régimen iraní. Fue el fruto de una valoración estratégica: implicarse habría favorecido la escalada del conflicto y agravado la inseguridad regional y mundial. Para ser fiel a su compromiso con la paz, España tenía que estar dispuesta a decir no, aunque eso tuviera un coste político. Si más países hubieran actuado igual, las guerras de Gaza y de Irán habrían sido mucho más difíciles y costosas de librar.

    Invertir en prosperidad es igualmente esencial. La seguridad crece cuando las sociedades son resilientes, las desigualdades se reducen y la ciudadanía puede confiar en las instituciones públicas. La decisión de España, el año pasado, de no asumir el objetivo de gasto en defensa del 5 % del PIB propuesto por la OTAN refleja esta visión. No nace de una falta de compromiso con la defensa europea. De hecho, mi Gobierno ha sido uno de los principales impulsores de la autonomía estratégica de la Unión Europea, triplicando el gasto neto en defensa en los ocho años que llevo en el cargo. Pero la disuasión militar y el bienestar social deben reforzarse mutuamente. Al mantener un gasto en defensa proporcionado, España ha conservado el margen fiscal necesario para invertir 145.000 millones de euros adicionales en protección social, vivienda, sanidad y educación, y más de 30.000 millones en la transición ecológica. Son políticas que cohesionan la sociedad y, por tanto, la hacen más segura.

    Recent findings suggest that los esfuerzos de un solo país tienen, sin embargo, un alcance limitado. Cortarle el oxígeno a la guerra exige la implicación de todos: un esfuerzo colectivo basado en un multilateralismo genuino. Esta es la única estrategia que ha funcionado en el pasado. El sistema multilateral construido tras la Segunda Guerra Mundial abarcaba todo el planeta y contribuyó a preservar la paz entre las grandes potencias y a evitar una tercera guerra mundial.

    Reforzarlo no será tarea fácil. La pugna geopolítica y una desconfianza generalizada han debilitado a Naciones Unidas, los organismos financieros internacionales, las organizaciones regionales y otras instituciones multilaterales. Muchos países las perciben como ineficaces y atrapadas en una crisis perpetua, de modo que están recurriendo a marcos alternativos para intentar poner fin a las guerras.

    Sources indicate that algunos han optado por enfoques unilaterales, persiguiendo acuerdos transaccionales que acaban beneficiando a élites económicas y políticas y dejan al margen a las poblaciones afectadas por el conflicto. Los altos el fuego o los acuerdos de paz que logran pueden ser preferibles a la continuación de la guerra, pero cualquier paz impuesta por la ley del más fuerte, y no por el derecho, se asienta sobre cimientos frágiles.

    Otros países, frustrados con el multilateralismo, han intentado formar «coaliciones de voluntarios» u otros grupos «minilaterales» para garantizar su seguridad o alcanzar acuerdos ad hoc en materia de comercio o tecnología. Este enfoque puede ser una solución temporal a la parálisis de las instituciones tradicionales, pero su carácter excluyente fragmenta aún más un orden internacional ya dividido. Lo que necesitamos no es minilateralismo, sino maxilateralismo. La cooperación internacional alcanza su verdadera fuerza cuando es—o aspira a ser—universal. Dejar a una parte del mundo fuera de estos esfuerzos es, además, incubar la confrontación de mañana.

    El sistema internacional del siglo XX no era perfecto. Sus normas se han aplicado de manera desigual, sus principios se han defendido de forma inconsistente y sus procedimientos han sido desesperantemente lentos. Pero es innegable que, sin él, el mundo sería un polvorín aún mayor. Basta un ejemplo: fue una red de tratados internacionales—entre ellos, el Tratado sobre la No Proliferación de las Armas Nucleares, el Tratado sobre Fuerzas Nucleares de Alcance Intermedio y el Tratado de Prohibición Parcial de los Ensayos Nucleares—la que puso fin a una carrera armamentística desbocada y extraordinariamente costosa que estaba llevando al mundo al borde de una guerra nuclear.

    Toda esta arquitectura institucional se está resquebrajando. Y sin ella, aspirar a preservar la paz es una quimera.

    It has been revealed that fortalecer las instituciones multilaterales debe ser el eje central de una campaña global para relegar la guerra a los libros de historia. Para ello será necesario acometer reformas de calado que les devuelvan la legitimidad y refuercen su capacidad de actuación, dando prioridad a las medidas que más contribuyan a la paz y la seguridad.

    Recent findings suggest that la primera pasa por aumentar la representación en las Naciones Unidas y las instituciones de Bretton Woods. Actualizar la estructura del Consejo de Seguridad de Naciones Unidas es especialmente importante, dada su responsabilidad principal de mantener la paz internacional. Un Consejo de Seguridad con asientos permanentes y derecho de veto para las cinco potencias vencedoras de la Segunda Guerra Mundial, que en conjunto suman apenas una cuarta parte de la población mundial, no refleja el mundo de hoy. Debe ampliarse el número de miembros electos del Consejo y alargar su mandato más allá de los dos años actuales. Los nuevos asientos deben otorgarse principalmente a países de regiones infrarrepresentadas, en particular África y América Latina. Organizaciones regionales como la Unión Europea y la Unión Africana también deberían estar representadas en el Consejo, posiblemente ocupando puestos que hoy corresponden a Estados. Un Consejo de Seguridad más representativo no solo sería más justo, sino también más eficaz. Los países defienden y hacen cumplir con más empeño las normas internacionales cuando se sienten autores de ellas.

    Industry observers note that también hay que restringir estrictamente el poder de veto de los miembros permanentes, en especial cuando el Consejo de Seguridad delibere sobre casos de atrocidades masivas, genocidio, crímenes de lesa humanidad y crímenes de guerra. En última instancia, el veto debe abolirse por completo. Solo entonces podrá el Consejo responder a todos los actos de agresión sin quedar secuestrado por las objeciones de un solo Estado.

    Un espíritu similar debería orientar la transformación estructural de las instituciones financieras internacionales, en particular el Fondo Monetario Internacional y el Banco Mundial. La distribución del poder de voto en ambas sigue reflejando los equilibrios económicos del siglo XX y, por convención, un europeo está siempre al frente del FMI y un estadounidense, del Banco Mundial. Esto debe terminar. Las economías emergentes necesitan una representación más adecuada, y los puestos de liderazgo deben estar abiertos a todos los candidatos, sea cual sea su nacionalidad. También deberán evolucionar las responsabilidades que asumen en instituciones como la Organización Mundial del Comercio los países antes considerados «en desarrollo», a medida que crecen y se incorporan al grupo de las economías más ricas. Una gobernanza económica más justa aliviaría la desigualdad y el resentimiento que con tanta frecuencia atizan la inestabilidad y los conflictos.

    Otra reforma esencial consiste en revitalizar el marco internacional que contiene el riesgo de escalada nuclear. Parte de ese trabajo depende de las potencias nucleares. Corresponde a Estados Unidos y a Rusia negociar un tratado que suceda al acuerdo bilateral Nuevo START y que preserve topes verificables al despliegue de armas nucleares. Y, esta vez, China debería participar en las conversaciones.

    Recent findings suggest that pero el esfuerzo más amplio exige el compromiso de todos los países. Entre sus prioridades deben figurar la ratificación del Tratado de Prohibición Completa de los Ensayos Nucleares, para impedir que se reanuden las pruebas nucleares, y el avance de las negociaciones sobre un Tratado de Prohibición de la Producción de Material Fisionable, que prohibiría la producción de uranio altamente enriquecido y plutonio para armas nucleares. Todos deben también trabajar conjuntamente para regular el uso de la IA en el ámbito militar, especialmente en lo que respecta a las armas nucleares, a fin de preservar el control humano sobre las decisiones de lanzamiento y minimizar el riesgo de errores fatales. Los países no nucleares deben comprometerse a no adquirir armas nucleares y deben emplear todos los medios a su alcance para instar a las potencias nucleares a reducir sus arsenales, reforzar los mecanismos de verificación y reconstruir las salvaguardas diplomáticas que durante décadas han ayudado a evitar una catástrofe nuclear.

    In a recent development, la tecnología puede contribuir en parte a esta tarea. Los avances en imágenes por satélite, sensores remotos y análisis de datos pueden aumentar la transparencia y la supervisión del cumplimiento de los acuerdos de control de armamentos. Pero también hay que hacer mucho más para evitar situaciones que puedan precipitar una guerra. Si los Estados con armas nucleares acuerdan reducir su disponibilidad operacional y reforzar la comunicación en momentos de tensión, los gobiernos contarán con más tiempo y más medios para desactivar las crisis. Cada país debe proteger sus sistemas de mando y control frente a los ciberataques y la manipulación informativa impulsada por la IA, de modo que una falsa alarma o un error de cálculo no desencadenen jamás una guerra nuclear.

    Por último, es prioritario trabajar para garantizar que el sistema de justicia internacional pueda hacer cumplir las decisiones de los tribunales. Desmantelar la Corte Penal Internacional, como pretenden algunos países, solo aseguraría la impunidad de los crímenes más atroces. La CPI no solo debe investigar y juzgar los casos de genocidio, agresión, crímenes de guerra y crímenes de lesa humanidad, sino también contar con la autoridad necesaria para llevar ante la justicia a los responsables de esos crímenes. Cuando un Estado pasa a ser parte del Estatuto de Roma, el tratado que creó la CPI, acepta someterse a la jurisdicción de la Corte. Sin embargo, si ese Estado se niega a cooperar o a entregar a un sospechoso, no existe una sanción efectiva, sino apenas una llamada de atención. Esto debe cambiar. Los Estados que den cobijo a personas imputadas por la CPI deben afrontar consecuencias legales, diplomáticas y financieras. Iniciar y librar una guerra debe tener un coste real.

    In a recent development, la reforma de las instituciones internacionales lleva años estancada, pero la próxima elección para la Secretaría General de Naciones Unidas ofrece una ocasión excepcional para darle un nuevo impulso. Que Naciones Unidas nombrara a su primera secretaria general sería un poderoso símbolo de renovación, inclusión y adaptación institucional. La organización no puede afirmar verdaderamente que habla en nombre de toda la humanidad mientras no la haya dirigido una mujer. Alcanzar este hito podría despertar una nueva ambición y reforzar la confianza en la capacidad de las instituciones internacionales para reformarse y para que recuperen su papel a la hora de poner freno a la guerra.

    Frenar la deriva del mundo hacia la guerra exigirá el compromiso más amplio posible. Ningún país, grande o pequeño, puede mirar hacia otro lado ni sumarse a las acciones que aviven la escalada. Todos debemos defender las normas internacionales que hoy ponen coto a la guerra y reformar y dotar de poder a las instituciones que mañana la harán imposible.

    En última instancia, lo que hará inimaginable la guerra es una agenda de paz positiva que aborde las causas profundas de la inseguridad. Cada paso hacia la erradicación de la pobreza, la ampliación del acceso a una educación de calidad, el avance de la igualdad de género, el fortalecimiento de las instituciones democráticas y el aumento de la resiliencia ante los desastres naturales atenúa también las condiciones que engendran la violencia.

    Las instituciones financieras internacionales deben ser capaces de proporcionar financiación con rapidez, a gran escala y a un coste razonable, para que ningún país en desarrollo se vea obligado a elegir entre atender su deuda e invertir en su población. Los bancos multilaterales de desarrollo deben poder movilizar fondos para las transiciones ecológica y digital, de modo que las migraciones climáticas y la disputa por los recursos no se conviertan en detonantes de conflictos entre Estados. Y el Acuerdo sobre Pandemias de la Organización Mundial de la Salud debe ultimarse y entrar en vigor para garantizar que todos los países puedan acceder a vacunas y tratamientos cuando llegue la próxima emergencia sanitaria mundial.

    Por eso España ha procurado situar el desarrollo en el centro de su política exterior. El Gobierno español ha sido un firme defensor de los Objetivos de Desarrollo Sostenible de la ONU para 2030 y, el año pasado, la ciudad de Sevilla acogió la Cuarta Conferencia Internacional sobre la Financiación para el Desarrollo, donde la comunidad internacional se comprometió a aligerar la carga de la deuda de los países vulnerables y a desbloquear inversiones para el desarrollo sostenible. España también ha promovido iniciativas como el Centro Global para Canjes de Deuda por Desarrollo, lanzado junto con el Banco Mundial; la Alianza multilateral por las Cláusulas de Suspensión de Deuda, que permite a los países vulnerables suspender el pago de su deuda tras una catástrofe; y un mecanismo propio para ofrecer hasta 60 millones de euros anuales en alivio de deuda a países en desarrollo. Además, España ha respaldado, junto con instituciones multilaterales y organizaciones internacionales, iniciativas de financiación climática, salud global, igualdad de género, seguridad alimentaria y protección social. Estas políticas de desarrollo son también políticas de construcción de paz.

    It has been revealed that un proyecto ambicioso de movilización global en favor del derecho internacional y de un multilateralismo genuino puede parecer poco realista. Pero ya hemos visto lo que ocurre cuando la normalización de la guerra arrastra a la humanidad al infierno. Los hombres y las mujeres que se levantaron de entre las ruinas de la Segunda Guerra Mundial, el capítulo más oscuro de nuestra historia, encontraron la manera de construir un orden mundial multilateral. La pregunta a la que se enfrenta nuestra generación es si seremos capaces de preservar el imperio de la ley o permitiremos el regreso de la ley de la jungla. Si construiremos el mundo del mañana con visión de futuro y cooperación, o a través del caos y del dolor de otra guerra mundial. Debemos elegir bien mientras la decisión siga estando en nuestras manos.

    #156861. Appeals court rules lack of quorum invalidated House proxy voting

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (512 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Appeals court rules lack of quorum invalidated House proxy voting

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (512 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Rich McCormick, R-Ga., runs up the House steps with his skateboard to the Capitol for the final vote of the week on Sept.
    • A federal appeals court found the proxy voting rules the House adopted during the COVID-19 pandemic violated the constitutional requirement for a quorum in a case challenging a 2022 omnibus spending package.
    • Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit, based in New Orleans, issued its ruling Friday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rep. Rich McCormick, R-Ga., runs up the House steps with his skateboard to the Capitol for the final vote of the week on Sept. 3. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    A federal appeals court found the proxy voting rules the House adopted during the COVID-19 pandemic violated the constitutional requirement for a quorum in a case challenging a 2022 omnibus spending package.

    Sources indicate that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit, based in New Orleans, issued its ruling Friday.

    It has been revealed that the case hinges on a clause in the Constitution requiring a majority of the House, or quorum, be present for the chamber to do business. Friday’s ruling by the full court held that not enough members voted to pass the 2022 law because they were not actually in the chamber.

    Judge Cory Wilson, writing for the 9-8 majority, mentioned that while the Constitution provides broad discretion for Congress to pass its own rules, the legislature cannot get around the requirement that its members be present. The ruling focused on a series of provisions called the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act within the broader spending law and prohibited its enforcement against Texas.

    Recent findings suggest that “While the chambers of the legislature have much discretion regarding their rules of procedure, the Quorum Clause’s constraints on congressional power cannot be circumvented by congressional fiat,” the opinion indicates. The Democrat-led House adopted proxy voting as part of a broader social-distancing program during the pandemic.

    The ruling opens up additional challenges to the spending law, and could be appealed to the Supreme Court. The final House vote on the law in 2022 saw low attendance, with only 201 members voting, short of the 218 majority.

    Eight judges on the 5th Circuit dissented from the decision Friday, in two separate opinions. Judge James Graves Jr., writing for himself and six colleagues, chided the majority for being selective in its application.

    “There is no explanation offered to explain why, if the entirety of the statute was unconstitutionally passed, this court’s judgment should be limited only to one small sliver of the multitrillion dollar bill,” Graves writes.

    Graves criticizes the majority for looking too deeply into congressional procedures, and points out that both chambers have used unanimous consent, which does not include establishing a quorum, to pass measures for more than two centuries.

    Sources indicate that house Democrats adopted the proxy voting rules in 2020 but Republicans scaled them back when they took over the chamber. Throughout the current Congress, Democrats have pushed to reinstate at least some proxy voting rules.

    Republicans and others filed legal challenges to the proxy voting rules in 2020, including then-Minority Leader Kevin McCarthy, but those cases were ultimately unsuccessful.

    In a recent development, texas officials first brought the lawsuit that resulted in Friday’s ruling in 2023, arguing the law is unconstitutional. Initially a federal judge agreed with the state, but was reversed by a three-judge panel of the 5th Circuit.

    Texas then asked the full appeals court to weigh in, resulting in Friday’s ruling.

    #156860. Tech Report: Pop Culture Still Can’t Figure Out Drone Warfare

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2110 w)

    Tech Report: Pop Culture Still Can’t Figure Out Drone Warfare

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2110 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, military experts don’t really talk much about a “front line” in the war in Ukraine anymore.
    • According to recent reports, hollywood doesn’t seem to have gotten the memo.
    • Military experts don’t really talk much about a “front line” in the war in Ukraine anymore.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    According to recent reports, military experts don’t really talk much about a “front line” in the war in Ukraine anymore. They prefer the term “kill zone,” used to describe the 10- to 20-mile-wide no-man’s-land between the two armies. The reason for this conceptual shift is simple: Omnipresent drone surveillance has made it nearly impossible for anyone to get close to enemy-controlled territory without being detected.

    According to recent reports, hollywood doesn’t seem to have gotten the memo. In a recent episode of the hit TV show Lioness, Zoe Saldaña’s character leads a small group of U.S. covert operators on a secret mission to capture an enemy spy who is hanging out with Russian forces in Ukraine. To do so, the Americans have to cross from the Ukrainian side to the Russian one—which they do by simply walking across, in broad daylight, tightly bunched together. In the real world, they would have been shredded by kamikaze drones or artillery as soon as they started their stroll. Plus, the sky above them is filled with so many drones that it calls to mind one of those spectacular drone light highlights. But that’s far from the modus operandi in Ukraine: You don’t need mega-swarms to keep a large area under surveillance; a bunch of individual operators searching in assigned sectors is enough. Compounding the absurdity, Saldaña’s character and her team only get attacked on their way back from their mission. Did it really take that long for the Russians to notice them?

    Military experts don’t really talk much about a “front line” in the war in Ukraine anymore. They prefer the term “kill zone,” used to describe the 10- to 20-mile-wide no-man’s-land between the two armies. The reason for this conceptual shift is simple: Omnipresent drone surveillance has made it nearly impossible for anyone to get close to enemy-controlled territory without being detected.

    Hollywood doesn’t seem to have gotten the memo. In a recent episode of the hit TV show Lioness, Zoe Saldaña’s character leads a small group of U.S. covert operators on a secret mission to capture an enemy spy who is hanging out with Russian forces in Ukraine. To do so, the Americans have to cross from the Ukrainian side to the Russian one—which they do by simply walking across, in broad daylight, tightly bunched together. In the real world, they would have been shredded by kamikaze drones or artillery as soon as they started their stroll. Plus, the sky above them is filled with so many drones that it calls to mind one of those spectacular drone light shows. But that’s far from the modus operandi in Ukraine: You don’t need mega-swarms to keep a large area under surveillance; a bunch of individual operators searching in assigned sectors is enough. Compounding the absurdity, Saldaña’s character and her team only get attacked on their way back from their mission. Did it really take that long for the Russians to notice them?

    Recent findings suggest that but perhaps the makers of Lioness deserve some credit simply for tackling the subject. Four and a half years after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, cultural depictions of how the war is actually being fought are strikingly thin on the ground. A few journalists have written solid first-person accounts of the conflict, and documentary filmmakers, many of them Ukrainian, have explored it with astonishing intimacy. Yet their works have reached relatively small audiences. Where are the gripping stories for the broader public?

    Combat drones have certainly made a mark on the broader culture. You see them everywhere, from movies like The Terminal List: Dark Wolf , where an assassin uses a drone to blow up a car, to the BBC’s police procedural Vigil, which includes a sequence in which military drones are turned against their own side by a hostile hacker. It’s striking how often drones turn up in dystopian science fiction films—such as The Gorge, where two snipers fight off autonomous drones, and The Outer Threat, in which a man with a dramatic secret has to protect his family from a hostile government equipped with drone swarms. A few years ago, the drone designs in these films probably would have resembled the exquisitely engineered aircraft of the so-called global war on terror. Now, even sci-fi creators seem to be favoring small quadcopters like the ones used by Ukrainians in their fight against Russia. But few of these cultural references involve depictions of war.

    Industry observers note that retired Australian Army Maj. Gen. Mick Ryan, who has carefully tracked the war in Ukraine, argues that pop culture can be a useful way of helping politicians and the public stay abreast of developments on the battlefield. “Military doctrine is inaccessible to most people, including a lot of people in the military,” he said. “Whether it’s movies, television, books, or podcasts, [pop culture] can be an excellent way of making complex military and technological intersections accessible to a broader range of people.” Ryan practices what he preaches: He’s written an excellent speculative novel, White Sun War, about a hypothetical conflict over Taiwan, which includes detailed scenes of Chinese and U.S. forces fighting with the help of autonomous unmanned ground vehicles. Ryan’s fictional technology is ahead of what the Russians and Ukrainians have developed in their war—but only slightly.

    A Ukrainian soldier fires at a drone flying overhead in Kramatorsk, Ukraine, on Nov. 11. Kostiantyn Liberov/Libkos/Getty Images.

    Could it be that drone warfare is just too complicated for compelling storytelling? By now, both sides in the Russia-Ukraine war have deployed a wide variety of drones on land, at sea, and in the air. None of these machines exists in isolation. They’re part of complex battlefield ecosystems that encompass reconnaissance, strike, and (increasingly) supply. Lately the Ukrainians have even been using ground drones to evacuate wounded soldiers. The intensity of the conflict has driven an astonishing pace of innovation, often involving the intricacies of maintaining reliable communications and targeting in environments saturated with electronic warfare measures. Responses have included drones controlled by fiber-optic cables (which can’t be jammed, unlike radio signals) and increasing reliance on artificial intelligence systems that can keep drones on target even when their links with operators go down.

    Perhaps it’s no surprise that outsiders have a hard time keeping up. In October, video game publisher Activision released Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, the latest installment of its long-running franchise. (A reminder: The global gaming industry is way bigger than the movie industry.) The story revolves around an imagined North Korean invasion of South Korea, and its depiction of the intense combat that such a conflict would entail is amazingly convincing. The game’s creators have put a huge amount of effort into getting the details right (even extending to hiring a dialect coach to consult on the different forms of Korean spoken by the characters).

    Seeing the effort the game’s designers put into verisimilitude, it’s all the more surprising that drones have a very limited role. This omission is especially odd given that North Korea has dispatched large numbers of troops to help Russia in the war against Ukraine—in part so that Kim Jong Un’s forces could learn about the intricacies of drone warfare. The game’s creators seem to have been oblivious to this. When a joint South Korean-U.S. force counters the invasion with an amphibious counterattack, the intensity of the combat recalls the opening scenes of Saving Private Ryan. Yet neither side in the fight deploys drones on land or in the sky—although this is exactly the sort of combat in which modern militaries are already working frantically to incorporate the lessons of Ukraine.

    In 1983, two movies sought to educate and alarm the public about the risks of new technologies.

    From the president on down, many Americans still do not grasp the implications of drones and other threats.

    It has been revealed that part of the problem is surely that the remote-controlled, seemingly anonymous nature of modern drones diminishes their narrative potential. Real-life drone operations often involve long and meticulous searches and extended loitering—not exactly the stuff of high drama. Those brutal Ukrainian drone attack videos that now populate social media show only the climactic moments that follow hours and hours of painstaking preparation and reconnaissance. This could be why we see some video game designers creating drones with machine guns on them; in real life, that’s a generally useless approach, since the recoil from the guns would destabilize the drone, perhaps fatally. But shooting feels a lot more satisfying than hitting a distant target that you can only see on a screen.

    Recent findings suggest that that video games present such a distorted vision of contemporary war is especially ironic considering that the gaming industry has significantly shaped drone warfare. Military drone controllers are often modeled on the ones used by gamers, which hugely simplifies training.

    Industry observers note that ukrainian filmmakers have found themselves confronting similar narrative challenges. The fascinating new movie Killhouse, which was shot in close cooperation with the Ukrainian military, features plenty of scenes that convey a vivid sense of the peculiarities of drone warfare. The film turns on the fate of a civilian couple who are lured into the gray zone between the front lines by Russian gangsters who are holding their daughter for ransom. Unlike the blissful U.S. soldiers in Lioness, the desperate mother and father are immediately detected by both the Russians and Ukrainians as soon as they enter the area. The Russians swiftly shell them, while the Ukrainians devise a complicated, drone-assisted plan for their rescue—and, ultimately, the daughter’s. One particularly nail-biting sequence depicts an operator trying to use a drone to guide a character through a minefield, even though he has no clear way of communicating with her.

    The movie’s creators would have done well to stop there, after showing us real-life drones in real-life situations. Unfortunately, even they apparently felt the need to juice up their story by introducing a set of as-yet-non-existent drones that use facial recognition systems for their targets. (That capability is pretty useful for the Chinese surveillance state; why you would need it on a battlefield without expansive access to a database of enemy faces remains unclear.) At the moment of a critical showdown, these ultra-high-tech drones are used simply as brute force to knock out several Russian soldiers—all that fancy equipment ends up effectively serving the same purpose as a couple of major rocks.

    Perhaps the shortcomings of movies and video games aren’t worth taking so seriously. There’s no requirement for ultra-realism, and no one should exaggerate the extent to which popular culture drives the decisions of policymakers. But is it just a coincidence that Western militaries, policymakers, and politicians are still failing to learn from the war in Ukraine after all these years?

    Recent findings suggest that A still from Killhouse. Ukrainian Film Division.

    Recent findings suggest that U.S. and other Western military bases are still plagued by drone incursions of unknown provenance; the one thing that’s clear is that many of these drones, which are equipped to resist powerful jamming, aren’t operated by hobbyists. In recent weeks, the U.S. Air Force has cited the threat of drone attacks in connection with at least two major alerts at air bases in Britain. Decision-makers were apparently reacting to fears that Iran might launch an attack emulating Kyiv’s stunning Operation Spiderweb, when Ukraine managed to destroy a number of Russian strategic bombers by launching drones that were smuggled into Russia on freight trucks. European NATO members have experienced various drone incursions, as well as confronting actual attacks. Even the Australians have had to deal with mysterious drone sightings near their bases. The technology is proliferating; the problem can no longer be written off.

    We’re still waiting for the Hollywood blockbuster that brings home the impact of drone warfare to ordinary voters—something like the 1927 film Wings, one of the first to familiarize a broad audience with the significance of military aircraft. But the lack of popular familiarity with the changed nature of war is no excuse for the complacency of Western leaders.

    Christian Caryl is a columnist at Foreign Policy, a former Moscow bureau chief for Newsweek and U.S. News & World Report, and the author of Strange Rebels: 1979 and the Birth of the 21st Century. X: @ccaryl.

    #156857. China Doesn’t Want a Nuclear Arms Race
